China's Q3 GDP Growth Seen Steady on Industrial, Export Strength as Domestic Demand Lags
Economists expect China to post stable third-quarter expansion, underpinned by solid industrial output and export performance, though more forceful measures to lift domestic demand will be essential for sustaining the recovery and hitting the annual growth objective, China Daily reported.
According to these analysts, high-tech manufacturing expansion and strong overseas demand continue to bolster the economy, yet weak household spending and an extended property market slump highlight the necessity of additional policy backing for more balanced expansion.
Before Monday's scheduled GDP figures for the third quarter, economists highlighted evidence of firmer activity in September. Wen Bin, chief economist at China Minsheng Bank, identified durable industrial production and lively exports as major growth supports.
The National Bureau of Statistics reported that the official manufacturing purchasing managers index climbed to 50.1 in September, returning to expansion after two consecutive months of contraction. Wen indicated this reading implies industrial output rose roughly 6 percent year-on-year in September.
High-tech manufacturing continued to anchor industrial expansion, with its PMI remaining above 52 across the third quarter and reaching 52.5 in September.
At the same time, strong foreign appetite for high-tech goods, driven by worldwide AI investment enthusiasm, gave exports fresh impetus. Data from the General Administration of Customs showed overall exports climbed 21.3 percent year-on-year in dollar terms during the first nine months, accelerating from 17.6 percent in the first half.
Lynn Song, chief economist for China at Dutch bank ING, said exports will probably stay a major growth driver through the remainder of the year.
A recent survey by media group Caixin showed third-quarter growth projections averaging 4.4 percent year-on-year, a modest rise from 4.3 percent in the prior quarter.
Domestic demand, however, stayed weak, and economists anticipate fixed-asset investment shrank further in the first nine months amid scant relief in the property downturn.
On Tuesday, the International Monetary Fund lowered its 2026 growth projection for China by 0.1 percentage point to 4.5 percent in its newest World Economic Outlook, citing elevated oil prices as an added burden on lackluster domestic demand.
Zhu Min, former deputy managing director of the IMF, argued that evaluating China's economy demands attention to both the growth rate and the structural shifts taking place, noting that new growth engines are already building momentum.
He added that the transition will require time, but structural changes should produce a healthier and more stable economy.
Zhu Feng, chief China economist and head of Greater China Economic Research at investment bank JPMorgan, cautioned that these emerging industries are still too small to rapidly substitute for the contribution previously provided by property and related sectors.
Authorities have intensified efforts to reinforce domestic demand as the economy transitions toward new growth drivers.
In late September, officials unveiled a targeted lending rate reduction and mortgage subsidies, after the State Council committed to introducing a package of practical and effective incremental policies aimed at achieving the full-year growth target of 4.5 to 5 percent.
More recently, the Ministry of Finance directed 550 billion yuan ($82.17 billion) in unused local government debt quotas to strengthen county and county-level district finances and back investment.
Xiong Yuan, chief economist at Guosheng Securities, said the extra funding, together with quicker fiscal spending since the third quarter, will provide further support for fourth-quarter GDP growth and should ensure full-year growth of at least 4.5 percent.
Luo Zhiheng, chief economist at Yuekai Securities, said growth may accelerate further if policy support progressively transmits to employment, household incomes, consumption and business investment.

KUALA LUMPUR – Australian tourist Cathy Hamilton was experiencing pangs of regret about her visit to Malaysia as she struggled to take pictures of the haze-shrouded Petronas Twin Towers.
“I tried to get some nice photos of the Twin Towers, Merdeka 118 and other scenery, but I couldn’t get good shots as they were all clouded by the haze,” said the Sydney native, who also struggled to breathe as smoke from Indonesia’s wildfires choked the region.
Had it not been for the ICU Asian Cheerleading Championships her daughters attended during the weekend, she probably would have cancelled her trip, Hamilton said earlier this week.
She is not the only tourist reconsidering Malaysia as haze blankets the country.
Tourism operators are experiencing fewer bookings for this time of year – and even cancellations – as smog disrupts flights, obscures some of the country’s best-known attractions and threatens a key driver of the South-east Asian economy.
Kuala Lumpur, Singapore and Jakarta were listed among the world’s 10 most-polluted major cities on Oct 20, according to live rankings from air-quality monitoring company IQAir. The bad air prompted schools to close in some parts of Malaysia.
Inbound tour operators are reporting cancellations for November and fewer group bookings, while overseas travel agents are seeking updates on air quality, according to Malaysian Inbound Tourism Association president Mint Leong.

articles.title: Ca Mau's economy in the first nine months of 2026: Fisheries, industry, and exports all growing. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: Ca Mau's economy in the first nine months of 2026: Fisheries, industry, and exports all growing.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
Besides the achievements, the progress of disbursing public investment capital (only reaching 52.8% of the plan) and the completion rate of some targets still need attention in the remaining months of the year.
 According to the report on socio -economic development in September and the first nine months of 2026 by the Ca Mau Provincial Department of Finance, production activities in the province continued to maintain growth momentum in many sectors. Fisheries played a significant role in the production structure, industry recorded a considerable increase, while exports and the consumer market continued to expand.
 Aquaculture continues to be a pillar of Ca Mau's economy. In the first nine months, the total aquaculture production reached 971,130 tons, equivalent to 72.7% of the plan, including approximately 275,230 tons from fishing and 695,900 tons from aquaculture. Shrimp production alone reached over 454,000 tons, an increase of 9.7%.
 The above results show that aquaculture production continues to maintain positive growth. However, considering the progress of the annual plan, aquaculture production after 9 months has only reached about 72.7% of the set target. This is an indicator that needs to be continuously monitored in the remaining months of the year, especially for aquaculture and fisheries activities.
 Along with aquaculture, rice production and other agricultural sectors remained basically stable. The total area planted with rice in the first nine months was estimated at over 280,500 hectares, with a yield of nearly 1,704,300 tons, equivalent to 91.1% of the plan. For the 2025-2026 Winter-Spring rice crop alone, the planted area reached 93,487 hectares, with an estimated average yield of 7.2 tons/ha, and a production of approximately 674,667 tons. 
 In the industrial sector, the industrial production index (IIP) in September increased by 11.6% year-on-year; the overall increase for the first nine months was 12.7%. Among key industrial products, processed shrimp continued to be a highlight with a production volume of nearly 305,300 tons, reaching 73.4% of the annual plan and increasing by 16.8% year-on-year.
 Electricity production is estimated at 6,459 million kWh, reaching 71% of the plan, an increase of 9.4%; commercial gas production reached 1,303 million m³, equivalent to 72.4% of the plan, an increase of 3.2%. These results contribute to the overall growth of industrial production in the area.
 Trade and export activities also recorded notable results. Total retail sales of goods and consumer service revenue in the first nine months were estimated at over 122,960 billion VND, equivalent to 75.6% of the plan, an increase of 19.4% compared to the same period last year. The Department of Finance assessed that the supply of goods remained basically stable, with no shortages or sudden price increases.
 Ca Mau province's total export turnover is estimated at nearly US$2.092 billion, equivalent to 74.7% of the annual plan and a 10.6% increase compared to the same period last year. Of this, seafood exports reached over US$1.8 billion, equivalent to 70.5% of the plan, a 5.1% increase. Fertilizer exports reached US$239 million, exceeding the plan by 29.2% and increasing by 82.2%; other goods reached US$47.6 million, a 10.3% increase.
 Financially, as of September 30, 2026, state budget revenue in Ca Mau province reached nearly 9,863 billion VND, equivalent to 86.5% of the projected target. Local budget expenditure reached over 16,888 billion VND, equivalent to 64.2% of the projected target.
 Conversely, the disbursement of public investment capital remains a key indicator requiring close monitoring. By the end of September, the province had disbursed nearly 5,449 billion VND out of a total planned 10,328.5 billion VND, reaching 52.8%. According to the Department of Finance, the province will continue to hold regular disbursement promotion conferences to review progress, urge departments and investors, and resolve difficulties and obstacles. 
 In terms of attracting investment, from the beginning of the year until now, the province has attracted 42 new projects with a total registered capital of over 40,633 billion VND; in September alone, there were 4 projects with a registered capital of over 8,547 billion VND. Cumulatively, the province has 731 active projects with a total registered capital of over 373,412 billion VND, including 31 FDI projects with a total registered capital of 4.95 billion USD.
 For the business sector, since the beginning of the year, 1,349 business registration certificates have been issued, an increase of 1.7% compared to the same period last year, with a total registered capital of VND 9,115.4 billion, an increase of 4.3%. The province currently has 10,130 operating businesses with a total registered capital of VND 130,033.2 billion.
 Regarding credit, by the end of September, mobilized capital of local credit institutions reached VND 99,500 billion, an increase of 7.9% compared to the end of 2025; outstanding credit reached VND 126,500 billion, an increase of 2.1%. The non-performing loan ratio is estimated at 2.9%.
 Overall, relatively strong budget revenue, large registered investment capital, and stable credit sources are positive signs. However, to maintain growth momentum and achieve the 2026 targets, Ca Mau province needs to continue accelerating the disbursement of public investment capital, supporting production and business activities, and promoting the progress of investment projects.

US warship sails near disputed Sabina Shoal in the South China Sea, triggering immediate response from Chinese Navy
More military posturing?
The United States Navy recently sailed a warship near the disputed Sabina Shoal in the South China Sea. This move triggered an immediate response from the Chinese Navy. Beijing officials accused the United States military of entering these waters without proper authorization. According to The Hill, the vessel involved is the USS Charleston, an Independence-class littoral combat ship. This ship currently operates out of Singapore as part of the Seventh Fleet.
Chinese officials claim that this action violates their sovereign rights. The Southern Theater Command Navy stated that they sent forces to track the American vessel. They claimed the ship “illegally intruded” into the area early on Tuesday, October 20, 2026. Yin Gang, who serves as the spokesman for the Southern Theater Command Navy, provided these details. He stated that the Chinese navy monitored and followed the USS Charleston during the patrol.
China asserts that it holds “indisputable sovereignty” over the Spratly Islands. They argue that the United States presence is “detrimental to regional peace and stability.” Beijing has demanded that Washington stop these activities immediately. This situation highlights the ongoing friction in the South China Sea. China claims roughly 90% of the sea as its own territory. This position leads to frequent disputes with nations like Malaysia, Vietnam, and the Philippines.
China has said the US’ presence in the disputed area is detrimental to regional peace and stability
The United States maintains that it conducts these missions to protect international shipping lanes. They call these actions freedom of navigation operations. The goal is to show that the region is not under the sole control of Beijing. This mission marks the first time this year that China has publicly accused a United States warship of entering these specific waters. Similar incidents have occurred in the past, such as in 2020 with the USS Montgomery.
The Philippines offers a different perspective on the event. According to the South China Morning Post, military spokesperson Vincent Trinidad denied that the American ship trespassed into Chinese territory. He stated that “no single nation has the authority to require prior permission for lawful transit through international waters.” This statement reflects the ongoing disagreements regarding maritime borders in the region.
Sabina Shoal sits about 145 kilometers northwest of the Philippine island of Palawan. It has become a significant flashpoint between Beijing and Manila since 2024. The Philippines stationed a coastguard vessel there for five months during that year. They were concerned about potential land reclamation efforts by China. That vessel eventually withdrew in September 2024. The withdrawal followed multiple confrontations between the two nations.
These tensions have included dangerous maneuvers and collisions between coastguard ships. One such altercation happened just last month near the same shoal. The Philippine Coast Guard claims that a Chinese ship rammed their boat. China disputes this account and blames the Philippines for the collision. The area is known as Xianbin Jiao in China and Escoda Shoal in the Philippines.
The United States remains a treaty ally of the Philippines
They have increased joint naval patrols and military exercises with Manila in recent years. This partnership aims to challenge what Washington considers excessive territorial claims by China.
Both the US and Philippines reaffirmed their relationship during the 12th United States-Philippines Bilateral Strategic Dialogue in February. They confirmed that the 1951 Mutual Defence Treaty covers armed attacks against public vessels. This treaty protection extends to coastguard ships operating anywhere in the Pacific, including the South China Sea.
The presence of the USS Charleston appears to be a calculated move by the United States. It comes ahead of a planned visit by President Donald Trump to Manila. Trump is expected to attend the ASEAN Summit in November. The Pentagon and the Navy did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the situation. The Seventh Fleet also remained silent on the specific details of the patrol.
Regional experts may view this incident as a sign of rising instability. The use of water cannons and physical collisions has become more common lately. Both sides seem firm in their conflicting interpretations of international law. China often demands that foreign vessels seek permission before entering these zones. The United States often rejects those demands as inconsistent with global maritime norms.
The situation at Sabina Shoal remains fluid
It seems unlikely that either side will back down from their stated positions soon. As the tensions rise, the international community watches with concern. Any further escalation could threaten the safety of vessels in this vital economic corridor. For now, the USS Charleston continues its deployment under Destroyer Squadron 7.
The incident serves as a reminder of the complex geopolitical reality in the South China Sea. Both Beijing and Washington continue to assert their influence in the region. The outcome of these naval encounters often shapes the broader diplomatic relations between the involved nations. It seems the reliance on military posturing will continue for the foreseeable future.

articles.title: Who Really Controls Agentic AI in Banking? - Fintech Singapore
articles.summary: Who Really Controls Agentic AI in Banking?  Fintech Singapore
articles.full_text:
How much control does a bank really have over the AI it uses?
Let’s picture a relationship manager reviewing a credit memo drafted by an agent.
Before relying on it, the banker first needs to know which customer records informed the assessment and whether the agent used the current lending policy.
And once other departments start building their own agents, keeping track of them becomes a job in itself.
As adoption spreads, teams may duplicate work, rely on different policy versions and struggle to track costs across departments.
Managing that work across departments is part of what Huawei aims to address with its Fintelligent AI Solution, which provides a shared foundation for developing and operating agents.
Huawei launched the solution at the Global Finance Summit during HUAWEI CONNECT 2026 in Shanghai on 18 September 2026.
Jason Cao, CEO of Huawei Digital Finance BU, presented Fintelligent as a way for banks to retain control over how they develop and use AI, explaining the thinking behind it in the company’s launch announcement.
“Every financial institution should own its AI and keep the choice and evolution of AI in its own hands.”
For a bank, this means retaining meaningful choice over its AI architecture and models, building reusable knowledge and agent assets, and maintaining the ability to operate and improve them over time.
Huawei’s approach includes making the agents and knowledge developed within a bank available for other teams to reuse.
Fintelligent connects these capabilities through an open hybrid AI architecture and three factories: Agent Factory, Token Factory and Data-Knowledge Factory.
Managing Agents Across the Bank
Cambridge’s 2026 research found that 81% of surveyed financial-services firms were adopting AI at some level, although just 14% considered it transformational to their organisational strategy and competitive advantage.
As an industry example, DBS’s credit-memo tool supports about 1,500 employees worldwide and handles more than 70 tasks associated with preparing the documents.
Relationship managers and credit risk managers review the drafts and remain responsible for the final memo.
Banks running these applications across departments need to establish who owns each agent and which systems it can access.
Huawei’s Agent Factory is built around openJiuwen, an open-source agent platform that provides a shared foundation for banks to develop, run, manage and govern agents.
openJiuwen supports banks in creating an Agent Marketplace where departments can share and reuse agents and skills developed across the institution.
Under the Monetary Authority of Singapore’s (MAS) AI risk guidelines, issued on 7 October 2026, financial institutions remain accountable for AI used in their services even when an outside provider supplies the technology.
MAS expects institutions to maintain inventories of their AI use and apply proportionate controls, including human oversight.
Institutions should meet the expectations in Sections 3–4 from 7 October 2027, and those in Sections 5–6 by 7 October 2028.
Managing the Cost of AI at Scale
Preparing a due diligence report can involve processing lengthy documents, whereas a banker checking an account detail during a customer conversation needs a quick response, making the choice of model and computing resources dependent on the job.
Huawei’s Token Factory solution, TokeNexus, supports token planning, production, scheduling and optimisation to help banks manage AI operating costs, performance and capacity.
Tokens are units of content processed by AI models.
Huawei describes both public-cloud and on-premises options, allowing banks to consider deployment approaches against their workload, security and performance requirements.
Cambridge found that 76% of surveyed large financial institutions struggled to measure the value of AI deployment.
Credit teams assessing the return could compare the cost of producing a memo with the time saved on preparation, accounting for the hours bankers still spend reviewing and correcting the draft.
Keeping Agents Aligned with Bank Knowledge
Policy updates need to reach agents as well as staff, because an agent working with an older document could apply rules the bank has already replaced.
Huawei’s Financial Agentic Data Solution, part of its Data-Knowledge Factory, supplies financial agents with data and knowledge drawn from institutional records, documents and rules.
Its pipelines are intended to keep supplying relevant material as the bank’s information changes.
Huawei also describes a path towards agent-assisted fraud operations, where investigators’ experience can be captured as reusable knowledge to support case analysis and rule refinement as fraud patterns evolve.
Preserving Business Rules in Legacy Systems
Business rules embedded in a bank’s software can determine how it assesses a customer’s loan, so developers need to preserve that logic when they replace the application.
Huawei’s AI Coding Solution helps them extract those rules as structured knowledge they can use in the replacement software.
Extracting those rules can help developers preserve business knowledge during modernisation, while the replacement application still requires validation.
These operational questions give practical meaning to owning AI.
The test is whether a bank can choose its technology, retain its business knowledge and keep improving its capabilities as adoption grows.

articles.title: Businesses need to prepare to seize opportunities from the Vietnam-EFTA Free Trade Agreement. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: Businesses need to prepare to seize opportunities from the Vietnam-EFTA Free Trade Agreement.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
|  | 
| Businesses need to control quality, ensure transparency in the supply chain, and comply with rules of origin for goods exported to the EFTA region. | 
 Businesses need to "act" now.
 After 14 years of negotiations, Vietnam and the European Free Trade Association (EFTA) signed the Vietnam-EFTA Free Trade Agreement (VEFTA) on October 18th. The agreement is currently awaiting ratification by member countries before it takes effect.
 EFTA is an intergovernmental organization promoting free trade and economic integration, currently comprising four members: Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway , and Switzerland.
 According to data provided by EFTA, bilateral trade between Vietnam and the bloc is projected to reach €4.8 billion in 2025, with Vietnam having a trade surplus of €2.5 billion. This result demonstrates that the trade relationship between the two sides has a solid foundation and opens up opportunities for businesses to further expand their markets.
 Leaders of the Ministry of Industry and Trade believe that cooperation with EFTA partners can help Vietnamese businesses enhance their competitiveness, gradually meet higher international standards, and participate more deeply in global value chains.
 As the 18th FTA signed by Vietnam, VEFTA opens up more opportunities to access the European market, but to turn these opportunities into actual orders, businesses need to proactively prepare early, instead of waiting for the agreement to officially come into effect.
 For exports, one of the key requirements is meeting the rules of origin to qualify for preferential tariffs under the agreements. Proper preparation of raw materials, documentation proving origin, and appropriate management processes will help businesses take advantage of these benefits and improve their competitiveness against goods from other exporting countries.
 VEFTA covers many areas, including trade in goods, tariffs, technical barriers, customs, trade defense, services, investment, intellectual property, dispute resolution, trade, and sustainable development. Therefore, the impact of the agreement lies not only in reducing import tariffs but also in its ability to promote investment cooperation, technology transfer, and improve governance capacity.
 Norwegian Ambassador to Vietnam Stein Iversen believes that the agreement will create more opportunities for Vietnamese goods to access the EFTA market, while also giving consumers on both sides more product choices.
 According to the Ambassador, the fact that Norwegian seafood products have access to the Vietnamese market with favorable tariffs is of significant importance to bilateral trade. Conversely, Vietnamese goods also have more opportunities to compete in EFTA markets.
 He recommended that Vietnamese exporters and manufacturers carefully study the agreement's content, proactively identify opportunities that match their products and capabilities, and take advantage of them as soon as the commitments are implemented.
 Opportunities go hand in hand with improving product quality.
 While the Vietnam-EU Free Trade Agreement (EVFTA) opens up opportunities to access a market of over 450 million people, and the CPTPP connects Vietnam with a vast economic space in the Asia-Pacific region and other continents, the VEFTA expands Vietnam's presence in markets with high purchasing power and stringent standards.
 EFTA has a population of approximately 15 million people, a relatively small size compared to the EU or CPTPP. However, the bloc's attractiveness lies in its high income levels and demand for high-quality products. This presents opportunities for Vietnamese industries with competitive advantages such as agricultural products, seafood, textiles, footwear, wood products, and electronics.
 In return, EFTA markets impose strict requirements on quality, food safety, environmental protection, and social responsibility. Businesses wishing to expand exports not only need to meet market access conditions but also ensure the stability and transparency of the entire supply chain.
 Swiss Ambassador to Vietnam Thomas Gass noted that consumers in Switzerland and EFTA countries are increasingly interested in product sustainability. Factors such as working conditions, water reuse, recycling efficiency, waste control, and reducing plastic waste in the environment are all considered important.
 According to the Ambassador, products that meet these requirements well can gain an advantage in the market, because consumers are willing to pay more for goods produced sustainably.
 Conversely, Vietnam has a market of over 100 million people, a strategic location in the Asia-Pacific region, and a wide network of FTAs. This is an advantage for Vietnam to become an investment and production destination, and a gateway for EFTA businesses to expand their operations in ASEAN and other regional markets.
 For the seafood industry, according to the Vietnam Association of Seafood Processing and Export (Vasep), the agreement should be seen as an opportunity to access additional markets with high purchasing power and quality requirements, aligning with the orientation of increasing export value rather than just chasing production volume.
 A representative from Vasep stated that VEFTA is a significant step forward for the seafood industry, but the benefits from the agreement do not automatically translate into business advantages. Opportunities will belong to businesses that are well-prepared in terms of quality, certification, traceability, rules of origin, packaging, labeling, and the ability to meet the requirements of importers, retail systems, and food service providers in Switzerland, Norway, and Iceland.
 "While awaiting the ratification of the agreement, businesses need to review their product portfolios, study tariff commitments and rules of origin, assess the technical requirements of each market, and complete certification documents and traceability systems," Vasep noted.

PENANG accounted for an average 64% of Malaysia’s exports of optical, precision, medical and surgical instruments, with RM238bil recorded from 2021 to the first half of 2026.
Chief Minister Chow Kon Yeow said nearly two out of every three ringgit Malaysia gained from these exports was earned in Penang.
“Medical technology (medtech) is no longer a niche sector here but a pillar of high-value manufacturing ecosystem.
“Penang is home to seven of the world’s top 30 medtech companies, including Abbott, Boston Scientific, B. Braun, STERIS, Smith+Nephew, Dexcom and Intuitive Surgical,” he said.
Chow said Penang secured RM2.3bil in approved manufacturing investments in the scientific and measuring equipment sector, including medical technology, across 40 projects from 2021 to the first quarter of 2026, creating nearly 4,500 jobs.
He said Penang’s medtech ecosystem had been built on more than 50 years of expertise in the electrical and electronics (E&E) sector.
“These competencies translate directly into surgical instruments, implants and high- accuracy medical devices.
“Penang did not build its medtech ecosystem from scratch.
“We built on the capabilities we already had and moved them into higher-value applications,” he added.
Chow said more than 20 local medtech companies produced devices registered by Medical Device Authority (MDA), ranging from orthopaedic implants and surgical instruments to wound care, dental products, infection- control solutions and medical consumables.
“Together, global leaders and homegrown champions give Penang one of the strongest concentrations of medtech capabilities in Southeast Asia, and position us alongside established offshore hubs such as Puerto Rico, Ireland and Costa Rica,” he said at the Medtech Industry Summit 2026 in Penang.
Deputy Investment, Trade and Industry Minister Sim Tze Tzin, who launched the summit, said Malaysia’s transition towards higher-value medtech would require greater localisation, deeper supply chains and stronger technology sharing between multinational corporations, local suppliers and startups.
“Local small SMEs gain access to high precision engineering standards, international certifications and technical know-how.
“This elevates the capabilities of domestic suppliers, turning local companies into world-class exporters,” he said.
Sim said Malaysia’s 17 free trade agreements (FTAs) comprising nine multilateral and eight bilateral agreements, also gave medtech companies access to markets covering about four billion people.
He urged companies to make greater use of the agreements to expand exports, while Malaysia was working towards an FTA with the European Union.
Sim also said the Government would continue supporting local suppliers through agencies including the Malaysian Investment Development Authority (Mida) and Malaysia External Trade Development Corporation (Matrade), particularly in supply-chain development, automation, technology adoption and access to export markets.
Meanwhile, Association of Malaysian Medical Industries (Ammi) chairman Samuel Pooranakaran said Penang had played a pivotal role in the country’s medtech success story.
“The state continues to foster a strong ecosystem for investment, innovation and talent development, further strengthening its position as a leading medtech powerhouse,” he said.
On Ammi’s Strategic Roadmap 2030, Samuel said it would provide a clear direction for the association and industry over the next five years.
“Our vision is to make Malaysia the leading global medtech ecosystem driven by talent, innovation and manufacturing excellence.
“Our key pillars – Policy Advocacy, Talent Development, Operational Excellence and Strategic Industry Partnerships and Development – continue to guide Ammi’s efforts to strengthen industry competitiveness, foster innovation, develop talent and support the long-term growth of Malaysia’s medtech ecosystem,” he added.
MDA chief executive officer Datuk Dr Muralitharan Paramasua said greater collaboration within the medical device industry was needed to strengthen the sector and expand its regional presence.
“We encourage the medical device industry to collaborate and hope the industries will grow in the region,” he said.
Dr Muralitharan said stronger cooperation between industry players, government agencies and other stakeholders would be important as Malaysia sought to deepen its medtech capabilities and move further up the value chain.

articles.summary: Attracting high-tech investment: Lessons from India for Vietnam  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
Backed by billions of dollars in subsidies, India's high-tech manufacturing sector is steadily integrating into global supply chains, but still faces challenges related to added value and investment efficiency.
This experience highlights the requirements for Vietnam in implementing Resolution 57: attracting investment must go hand in hand with enhancing endogenous technological capacity and mastering high-value-added stages.
Optimists argue that Apple's move to shift some iPhone production to India helps the country reduce its dependence on China and improve its position in the global supply chain. Currently, about a quarter of iPhones are manufactured in factories near Chennai, providing jobs for tens of thousands of workers.
However, skeptics argue that much of the activity remains focused on final assembly, which creates little added value. Nevertheless, Indian factories have begun taking on more stages, from assembling components onto circuit boards to manufacturing motherboards.
The core question is whether these advances are commensurate with the state subsidies. If competitiveness cannot be maintained without budgetary support, the gains of India's manufacturing sector risk reversing.
Moving deeper into the global supply chain.
Smartphones use many high-value components such as circuit boards, camera modules, and screens. To truly improve its position in the production chain, the export value of finished phones needs to increase faster than the import of input components.
However, the evaluation is not simple because many imported components are also used in electric vehicles , solar panels, and other equipment.
In 2023, former Reserve Bank of India Governor Raghuram Rajan and two colleagues developed three scenarios, assuming that 40%, 60%, or 80% of imported components in the multipurpose category were used in mobile phones. In all three cases, India's mobile phone trade balance remained in deficit. The research team argued that the increase in finished phone exports was not enough to demonstrate that the country's manufacturing capacity had reached a breakthrough.
Newer analysis shows that the trade balance remains in deficit, but the gap between component imports and phone exports has narrowed. This indicates progress in domestic manufacturing, although it is not yet possible to say that India has mastered the majority of the product's value.
Value added remains limited.
You may also like
Indian suppliers have expanded into more complex processes, but the lack of mastery in the production of memory chips, processors, lenses, displays, and batteries still limits the ability to create domestic value.
With the iPhone 14, India narrowed the production gap with China to just two months, up from six to nine months previously. The iPhone 15 was the first model Apple manufactured in India to be ready for the global launch from day one.
Suppliers, including Foxconn, have also shifted from importing complete circuit boards to assembling components directly in India. Motherboard manufacturing alone is expected to improve the trade balance by $2.1 billion in the 2025-2026 fiscal year.
However, the outlook remains uncertain. Strong demand for memory chips from data centers is driving up the price of semiconductors used in phones. Meanwhile, demand for phones in the Indian market is declining, especially in the low-cost segment. This could reduce component imports, but weaker global smartphone sales also risk impacting exports.
Subsidies are putting increasing pressure on the budget.
Five years ago, India implemented a subsidy program equivalent to 4-6% of the finished phone bill value to offset infrastructure disadvantages and production costs. As chip prices rise due to demand from the artificial intelligence (AI) sector, the budget may have to bear additional support costs.
With a subsidy rate of 4%, for every additional $1 billion in the bill value solely due to rising chip prices, the budget would have to spend an extra $40 million. Thus, even if production doesn't increase proportionally, the cost of subsidies could still balloon.
To move further into the supply chain, the Indian government has allocated an additional $13.4 billion to develop the domestic semiconductor industry. However, the $10 billion subsidy introduced five years ago has mainly helped establish overseas chip packaging facilities, failing to create advanced chip manufacturing capabilities.
Advanced chip manufacturing requires cutting-edge technology, significant capital investment, and the ability to accept long periods without profitability. India still faces challenges in all three areas. Even Tata Group, a key Apple partner in the country and the company behind India's only semiconductor manufacturing plant project, is facing disputes over control and concerns related to the scale of investment in the electronics sector.
International experience shows that moving up to higher-tech stages is not easy. Malaysia developed chip packaging and circuit board assembly operations from the 1970s, but its progress up the value chain stalled after the country reached upper-middle income status in 1992. Meanwhile, South Korea and Taiwan (China) leveraged the semiconductor industry to rise to the ranks of wealthy economies.
It's not easy to copy the Chinese model.
India can hardly rely solely on billions of dollars in investment to quickly catch up with the world's leading high-tech manufacturing hubs. Instead, it needs to develop its design and engineering capabilities while allocating resources to healthcare, education, climate change response, and labor-intensive industries such as textiles, footwear, and toys.
You may also like
The Chinese model is particularly difficult to replicate. Apple's success in the country is linked to Foxconn's ability to coordinate with local authorities to rapidly build large-scale factory complexes. This combination of deployment speed, production scale, and risk tolerance is an advantage that India will find difficult to replicate.
Apple may be able to help India improve its manufacturing capabilities and become more deeply involved in the global supply chain, but that doesn't mean the country will become the next factory of the world. Continuing to increase subsidies in the hope of replicating the Chinese model could lead to ever-increasing costs without necessarily delivering commensurate benefits.
From attracting investment to mastering technology: Lessons for Vietnam
Drawing lessons from India's experience, Vietnam can develop high-tech industries in line with the spirit of Resolution 57-NQ/TW dated December 22, 2024, of the Politburo on breakthroughs in national science, technology, innovation, and digital transformation. Investment incentives may attract large corporations, but they cannot replace endogenous technological capabilities and the ability to master high value-added processes.
Therefore, support policies need to be linked to tangible results such as technology transfer, development of supporting industries, training of high-quality human resources, and enhancement of research, design, and manufacturing capabilities. Regular evaluation of budget utilization efficiency is also essential to limit prolonged reliance on incentives without building sustainable competitiveness.
More importantly, Vietnam needs to focus on investing in research and development, digital infrastructure, education, and linkages between businesses and research institutions. This is the foundation for science, technology, and innovation to truly become a driving force for productivity enhancement, helping domestic businesses move up to higher value-added stages in the global supply chain, instead of primarily relying on processing and assembly.

Citi has pledged to work more closely with Vietnam’s Ministry of Finance to improve the country’s sovereign credit rating and strengthen its standing in global financial markets, while seeking funding solutions to support the development of Vietnam’s energy sector.
Ernesto Torres Cantú, Citi’s head of International and a member of the group's Executive Management Team, made the remarks during a meeting with Vietnam's Deputy Prime Minister Nguyen Van Thang in Hanoi last Friday.
Citi sees significant opportunities to contribute further to Vietnam’s efforts to achieve its growth targets, Cantú was quoted by the Vietnamese government's news portal as saying.
He thanked Vietnamese authorities for their strong support, adding that this assistance would enable Citi to make a greater contribution to the country’s development.
Citi’s leadership also praised the Vietnamese government for its efforts to improve the business environment, saying the group’s engagement with regulators had become increasingly convenient and open.
Bringing international investors to Vietnam is Citi's mission, Cantú said, adding that the group stood ready to help Vietnamese businesses access international markets.
Deputy Prime Minister Thang said the government was firmly committed to achieving average annual GDP growth of at least 10% during the 2026-2030 period while maintaining macroeconomic stability.
The economy had shown very positive signs over the first nine months of the year and received strong assessments from international organizations, he said. Realized foreign direct investment exceeded $21 billion during the period, up 76.4% from a year earlier, "reflecting strong foreign investor confidence in Vietnam’s business environment".
He praised Citi for maintaining stable, safe and efficient operations in Vietnam and complying with local laws, demonstrating "a cooperative approach and proactive risk management".
The deputy prime minister thanked Citibank for providing modern financial solutions in corporate banking, trade finance and cash management, as well as for implementing community programs focused on education and skills development that deliver practical benefits to Vietnamese society.
As Vietnam and the United States continue to advance their Comprehensive Strategic Partnership, Vietnam values long-established U.S. businesses such as Citi and hopes they will continue to serve as a bridge for attracting high-quality investment and helping Vietnamese companies connect with global financial networks, Thang said.
The Vietnamese government values foreign businesses, listens to their concerns and stands ready to facilitate long-term, effective investment and operations in the country, particularly by major U.S. financial institutions such as Citi, he added.
Thang said Vietnam’s ambitious growth targets required the mobilization of all available social resources, including funding from international financial institutions.
He called on Citi to continue sharing international expertise and working closely with Vietnamese regulators on digital transformation, international payments and solutions to support sustainable business development.
The Vietnamese leader also urged Citi, as a global financial institution, to support Vietnam in developing the International Financial Center, located in both Ho Chi Minh City and Danang.
He further called on the bank to convey to the U.S. government Vietnam’s goodwill and commitment to cooperation in efforts to conclude negotiations on a reciprocal, fair and balanced trade agreement at an early date, in the interests of businesses and people in both countries.
Noting that Vietnam will host APEC 2027, Thang called on Citi to send a senior leadership delegation to the APEC CEO Summit and work closely with the Vietnamese government to ensure the successful organization of the event.
APEC 2027 is expected to help Vietnam further open its markets, attract investment, facilitate technology transfer, and strengthen the competitiveness of its economy, he added.

articles.title: Vietnam-EFTA Free Trade Agreement: A strategic milestone opening a new era of cooperation. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: Vietnam-EFTA Free Trade Agreement: A strategic milestone opening a new era of cooperation.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
VTV.vn - The signing of the Vietnam-EFTA Free Trade Agreement after 14 years of negotiations marks a historic milestone, opening up opportunities for breakthrough economic, trade, and investment cooperation between Vietnam and four European countries.
A historic milestone after 14 years of negotiations.
On the morning of October 18, 2026, in Hanoi , in the presence of General Secretary and President To Lam, Minister of Industry and Trade Le Manh Hung, along with representatives from member countries of the European Free Trade Association (EFTA), officially signed the Vietnam-EFTA Free Trade Agreement (VEFTA). This historic signing is the culmination of 14 years of persistent negotiations, including 21 official rounds of talks between the two sides.
The VEFTA agreement is considered a new generation FTA with a comprehensive scope of commitments and very deep openness. The agreement covers core areas including trade in goods (including tariffs, technical barriers to trade (TBT), sanitary and phytosanitary measures (SPS), customs and trade defense), trade in services, investment, intellectual property, government procurement, competition, support for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), dispute resolution, as well as trade and sustainable development.
Strategic significance in the context of a volatile global geo- economic landscape.
Assessing the strategic significance of the VEFTA Agreement for bilateral relations in the context of a complex global economic landscape, Swiss Ambassador to Vietnam Thomas Gass emphasized the importance of returning to fundamental principles: "We are living in a world strongly disrupted by geo-economics and geo- politics , and in that context, it is extremely important to return to fundamental principles. The fundamental principle is that if we have agreed on a method of trade, we will strictly adhere to that method, so that both sides can trust each other. Any business needs predictable stability and trust. That is what we want to build between Switzerland, other EFTA countries, and Vietnam. We want to ensure that when Swiss companies invest in Vietnam, when they cooperate commercially with Vietnam, they know exactly what they will receive. And when Vietnamese businesses begin trading with Swiss companies, they also know exactly what they will receive." What will be gained? That's the essence of the matter; that's strategic value. This is especially important, particularly in today's world."
You may also like
From a diplomatic perspective, Mr. Stein Iversen, the Norwegian Ambassador to Vietnam, affirmed that the agreement will become a "cornerstone" in the relationship between the two countries, taking bilateral relations to a new level: "Clearly, the free trade agreement will become a 'cornerstone' in our relationship with Vietnam. The agreement will take our relationship to a new qualitative level. From Norway's perspective, we also have the Green Partnership, the Green Strategic Partnership, which was signed last April. And for us, this partnership provides a political framework for the road ahead, moving forward together. Therefore, combined with the 55th anniversary of the establishment of diplomatic relations, which Switzerland and Norway are jointly celebrating, and alongside this free trade agreement, this is truly a milestone in our relationship with Vietnam and represents a significant step forward for us."
Potential for collaboration and breakthrough opportunities for businesses.
Besides strategic direction, the VEFTA agreement is expected to open up concrete business cooperation opportunities in many key economic sectors. Analyzing the most potential areas of cooperation between Switzerland and Vietnam, Swiss Ambassador Thomas Gass shared: "In reality, there are many areas. Switzerland is perhaps the most innovative country in the world, and this innovation can truly benefit the Vietnamese economy, helping Vietnamese products achieve top quality and operate very effectively in the global value chain and on the world market. I'm thinking of the automotive industry, where some Swiss companies produce giant molding machines where you can print the chassis (skateboard) of an electric car in just one step."
We want to ensure that Vietnam becomes a global player in the services sector, not only in finance but also in information technology (IT tech). We currently have several Swiss companies operating in Da Nang, Ho Chi Minh City, and Can Tho providing world-class IT services, including IT programming services for the banking and insurance industries. All of this can be expanded under free trade agreements."
Regarding market access and the practical impact of tariff reductions, Norwegian Ambassador Stein Iversen emphasized the direct benefits that businesses and consumers on both sides will receive: "Tariffs will move closer to 0% for the vast majority of goods traded between Vietnam and EFTA countries. And especially for Norwegian seafood exports, the agreement will significantly reduce tariffs to 0%, as in the case of salmon, making salmon more accessible to Vietnamese consumers. Conversely, the Norwegian market will become more accessible to Vietnamese exporters for items such as processed coffee, fruits, tropical fruits, and in the textile industry."
New drivers for value chain growth and sustainable development.
The official signing of the VEFTA Agreement marks a historic milestone, creating a safe, transparent, and stable legal framework for investors. For Vietnamese businesses, cooperation with leading partners from EFTA not only increases import and export turnover but also provides a valuable opportunity to access high technology, improve management capacity, and meet the stringent sustainable development standards of the global market. The support of the governments and business communities of both sides promises to usher Vietnam-EFTA economic cooperation into an era of dynamic, comprehensive, and sustainable development.
You may also like
The EFTA bloc comprises four countries: Switzerland, Norway, Iceland, and Liechtenstein – leading economies in innovation, finance, and high technology. Over the years, economic, trade, and investment cooperation between Vietnam and EFTA countries has continuously developed positively. Bilateral trade turnover averages nearly US$2 billion annually. In 2025 alone, two-way trade turnover is projected to reach €4.8 billion, with Vietnam recording a trade surplus of €2.5 billion.
The structure of goods traded between Vietnam and EFTA is clearly complementary. Vietnam's main exports to the EFTA bloc are strong products such as seafood, textiles, footwear, machinery and equipment, electronics and components. Conversely, Vietnam imports from EFTA industrial machinery, high-tech equipment, chemicals, pharmaceuticals and raw materials for production.
Regarding investment cooperation, by the end of 2025, Switzerland had 234 direct investment projects in Vietnam with a total registered capital of over US$2.4 billion. Norway currently owns 62 projects with a total registered capital of over US$201 million. Many leading economic groups from the EFTA bloc have a long-term presence and operate effectively in Vietnam, while continuing to expand investment in new areas such as logistics, precision engineering, high technology, and innovation. With a market size of over 100 million people and a network of 17 established free trade agreements, Vietnam is a strategic bridge for EFTA businesses to expand throughout the ASEAN region.

A credit package of 15 trillion VND for businesses in priority sectors.
In line with the government and State Bank of Vietnam's operational guidelines,VIB proactively adjusted deposit interest rates downwards by up to 0.5 percentage points per year, based on balancing various maturities, focusing on those with maturities exceeding 6 months. Simultaneously, the bank reduced operating costs and balanced its deposit and lending sources to create room for further cost reductions for customers.
In lending activities, VIB continues to reduce interest rates compared to the current interest rate schedule for new loans to corporate customers. Specifically, the bank has just launched a preferential credit package worth VND 15,000 billion for businesses in priority sectors, applying preferential interest rates under the program, reduced by up to 1.5% per year depending on program conditions.
Credit granting is considered on a case-by-case basis for each customer, linked to requirements for ensuring credit safety and quality. The focus is on businesses in sectors and fields encouraged and prioritized by the State, such as: supporting industries for the production of materials, components, and spare parts; infrastructure; public investment; renewable energy; and exports.

articles.title: Singapore and UAE to start talks on economic pact, form joint energy task force - The Straits Times
articles.summary: Singapore and UAE to start talks on economic pact, form joint energy task force  The Straits Times
articles.full_text:
SINGAPORE – Singapore and the United Arab Emirates (UAE) are set to begin talks on a comprehensive economic partnership agreement that seeks to create new opportunities for businesses on both sides.
The deal, which is similar to a free trade pact, will facilitate trade and investment flows and deepen economic integration between the two nations, said the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MFA) in a statement on Oct 21.
Prime Minister Lawrence Wong and UAE President, Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, announced plans to start negotiations on the agreement at a meeting in Abu Dhabi between ministers and senior officials from both sides.
The Oct 21 meeting was part of PM Wong’s five-day visit to the Middle East, which started on Oct 18 in Qatar.
At the meeting, Singapore and the UAE also agreed to form a joint energy task force to identify fresh opportunities across the energy value chain, from trading to infrastructure to downstream activities.
The task force comprising Singapore’s Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry and the Abu Dhabi National Oil Company will come under the scope of the Abu Dhabi-Singapore Joint Forum (ADSJF), said MFA.
The ADSJF, which held its 17th edition in Singapore in September, is an annual platform for both countries to strengthen their economic ties and explore new areas of shared interest.
Singapore and the UAE said in a joint statement that the task force is part of efforts to strengthen bilateral cooperation on enhancing energy security and supporting their energy transition ambitions.
They added that both sides welcome their ongoing cooperation in nuclear energy – the Emirates Nuclear Energy Company and Singapore’s Energy Market Authority had inked a deal in 2024 to collaborate in developing nuclear energy capabilities.
Another agreement from the meeting seeks to enhance collaboration between Singapore and the UAE on water management, water technology development and capability building.
The renewal of the deal, which was first inked by national water agency PUB and the Abu Dhabi Department of Energy in 2018, will also strengthen cooperation in advancing water sustainability and resilience, said PUB on Oct 21.
PUB said in response to queries that the 2018 pact has created opportunities for Singapore firms in Abu Dhabi. It cited engineering consultancy Meinhardt, which has offered water-related training and capability development, and water tech firm ZWEEC, which has applied its fish activity monitoring systems for real-time water quality monitoring.
PUB said the refreshed pact will expand collaboration into areas such as managing water resources and water demand and deploying innovative water technologies.
Under the pact’s widened scope, both sides will also cooperate on climate change mitigation and adaptation and joint research and innovation, while piloting and test-bedding innovative water technologies, among other initiatives, said PUB.
Both countries said in their joint statement that they are keen on exploring new opportunities to share knowledge and forge partnerships to develop and deploy sustainable and scalable water solutions.
Another deal was signed by Singapore’s National Environment Agency (NEA) and the Abu Dhabi Public Health Centre (ADPHC) to exchange knowledge, technical expertise and operational insights on controlling vectors to safeguard public health. Vectors are organisms, such as mosquitoes, rodents and cockroaches, that transmit disease-carrying pathogens.
The deal will inform the ADPHC’s development and use of a method to suppress the Aedes aegypti mosquito population in Abu Dhabi called the incompatible insect technique, said NEA.
The collaboration will draw on NEA’s efforts to control the Aedes mosquito population in Singapore through Project Wolbachia, added the agency.
At the meeting, the two nations also agreed to explore cooperation in other areas, including defence, artificial intelligence and digitalisation.
On Oct 21, PM Wong was received by Sheikh Mohamed at the Qasr Al Watan, where he was welcomed with a ceremony. He was also hosted to lunch by Sheikh Mohamed.
In a social media post later that day, PM Wong said Singapore stands with the UAE as a trusted partner and friend during what has been a “difficult period” for the UAE and the wider Middle East.
He said he had spoken with Sheikh Mohamed to express the Republic’s solidarity with and support of the UAE soon after the Middle East conflict broke out in March, and thanked him for looking after Singaporeans in the Emirates.
Both leaders also exchanged views on regional developments and the importance of restoring peace and stability in the region, said PM Wong.
“In an increasingly troubled world, our partnership matters more than ever. By working together and combining our complementary strengths, we can achieve far more than either of us could on our own,” he added.
PM Wong said he looks forward to welcoming Sheikh Mohamed to Singapore for a state visit and working with him to enhance bilateral ties.
The two leaders also agreed to convene the fourth Singapore-UAE Joint Committee to review the progress of their comprehensive partnership, which was established in 2019, and identify new areas of cooperation.
In their joint statement, both countries said they also welcome the opportunity presented by Singapore’s upcoming chairmanship of ASEAN in 2027 and the third ASEAN-Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) Summit to enhance cooperation between both regions.
This includes advancing discussions on a ASEAN-GCC free trade agreement, they said. The UAE is one of six members of the GCC.
Later on Oct 21, PM Wong travelled to Dubai, which is the final stop of his trip to the Middle East.
He is scheduled to meet UAE Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance, Sheikh Maktoum bin Mohamed bin Rashid Al Maktoum.
PM Wong is also set to attend a reception for overseas Singaporeans in Dubai before his trip ends on Oct 22.
The UAE is Singapore’s largest trading partner in the Middle East. In 2025, bilateral trade in goods hit $27.9 billion, and bilateral trade in services reached $12.8 billion in 2024.

articles.title: Sabeco sets sights on expanding investment in central Vietnam province Quang Ngai - Theinvestor
articles.summary: Sabeco sets sights on expanding investment in central Vietnam province Quang Ngai  Theinvestor
articles.full_text:
Alongside its brewery in Quang Ngai, Sabeco is expanding into commercial services and leasing, while exploring a potential social housing project in the central Vietnam province.
From brewery to commercial and service projects
Saigon Beer-Alcohol-Beverage Corporation (Sabeco), a top beer maker in Vietnam, has operated in Quang Ngai since 2005 through Saigon Beer-Quang Ngai Joint Stock Company (BSQ), one of its subsidiaries in central Vietnam.
In 2007, BSQ was granted an investment certificate to build the Saigon Beer-Quang Ngai brewery in Quang Phu Industrial Park, with a total investment of more than VND1.58 trillion ($61.06 million) and an initial designed capacity of 100 million liters of beer per year.
Construction began in 2009, with the first phase completed in December 2010. The company subsequently invested in additional production lines, fermentation systems and energy-saving solutions to increase capacity and improve product quality.
Between 2018 and 2021, the brewery underwent further upgrades and expansion, raising its capacity to 250 million liters per year. In March 2022, the facility produced its first batches of beer following completion of the capacity expansion project. In the first eight months of 2026, BSQ produced more than 98.6 million liters of beer, equivalent to over 88% of the year's target. Export revenue was estimated at $1.84 million.
Beyond beer production, BSQ is expanding into commercial services through a shopping, service and leasing center project at 06 Nguyen Thuy street in Nghia Lo ward, Quang Ngai province.
Construction began in June 2026, with the basic construction phase expected to be completed in March 2027. The project covers more than 7,800 square meters, with a building density of 55%, three storeys and a total floor area of more than 10,200 sqm. Planned facilities include entertainment, shopping and dining areas.
Following several capital increases, the project now has a total investment of more than VND302 billion ($11.67 million). The development marks a step towards diversifying BSQ's investments beyond beer production while adding commercial and entertainment services in Quang Ngai.
Sabeco is also looking at further investment opportunities in the province.
At a recent meeting with Quang Ngai provincial leaders, Sabeco general director Lester Tan Teck Chuan thanked the local authorities for their attention and support. He reaffirmed the company's commitment to working with the province to sustain and expand its business operations and contribute to local socioeconomic development.
Going forward, Sabeco plans to continue expanding its investments in Quang Ngai, explore a social housing project and bring the shopping, service and leasing center into operation.
The company also plans to raise its production capacity to 350 million liters per year in the coming period, strengthen its brands, and expand sales in Quang Ngai and nationwide.
Profit surges in first half
According to BSQ's interim financial statements for the six months ended June 30, 2026, net revenue from sales of goods and provision of services reached VND858.9 billion ($33.19 million), up 4% from the same period in 2025.
Higher revenue and lower cost of goods sold helped more than double gross profit to VND93.9 billion ($3.63 million). After expenses, BSQ reported net profit of VND62.8 billion ($2.43 million), compared with VND21.5 billion ($830,820) a year earlier.
As of June 30, 2026, BSQ's total assets stood at nearly VND1.21 trillion ($46.6 million), slightly lower than at the beginning of the year. Cash and cash equivalents amounted to VND47.6 billion ($1.84 million), an increase of more than VND38 billion from the start of the year.
The company also held more than VND44 billion ($1.7 million) in short-term financial investments, while short-term receivables stood at VND169.7 billion ($6.56 million) and inventories at approximately VND176.6 billion.
Total liabilities exceeded VND350 billion ($13.53 million), edging up from the beginning of the year. All liabilities were short-term.
Recently, the Quang Ngai provincial tax authority issued an administrative penalty against BSQ for tax violations.
The authority found that the company had incorrectly declared taxes, resulting in underpayments of corporate income tax for 2020 and 2021, value-added tax for the June and August 2020 tax periods, and personal income tax for 2020, 2021 and 2022.
BSQ was fined a total of nearly VND74.48 million ($2,880) for the violations. In addition to the fine, the company was ordered to pay more than VND768 million ($29,680) in additional tax assessments and more than VND419 million in late-payment interest.

Listen to this article in summarized format
EFTA comprises Switzerland, Norway, Iceland and Liechtenstein, which are not EU members. The agreement was signed in Hanoi by senior representatives of the four EFTA states, including Swiss President Guy Parmelin, and by Vietnam's Minister of Industry and Trade Le Manh Hung, according to an EFTA document. Its entry into force is pending, the document said.

Bilateral trade between EFTA and Vietnam was EUR 4.8 billion in 2025, with a surplus of EUR 2.5 billion in Vietnam's favour, up from EUR 0.5 billion a decade earlier, according to EFTA. Electrical machinery, footwear and apparel, and mechanical machinery were the top imports from Vietnam.
India's Trade and Economic Partnership Agreement (TEPA) with EFTA was signed on March 10, 2024, and came into force on October 1, 2025. EFTA offered market access on 92.2% of its tariff lines, covering 99.6% of India's exports. India opened 82.7% of its tariff lines, covering 95.3% of EFTA's exports, according to the Press Information Bureau (PIB).
Ajay Srivastava, founder of the Global Trade Research Initiative (GTRI), said the deal will not affect India's exports. "EFTA countries levy zero tariffs on industrial products, so deal with Vietnam or any other country including India offers no additional tariff advantage in these markets," he said. Competition will depend on product quality, price and delivery reliability, he said.
Normal route or FTA route
EFTA's free trade dashboard says Iceland and Norway abolished tariffs on most industrial imports on their own, and Switzerland and Liechtenstein did so from January 1, 2024.
Preferences under an FTA are not automatic, the dashboard says. Importers must claim them, and goods must meet the agreement's rules of origin. It calculates preference utilisation only on the subset of trade where a preferential margin exists. Its data covers 2018 to 2024, before India's pact took effect.
India's exports to EFTA
Dhar said Vietnam's duty-free access to EFTA countries poses a significant challenge to India's ambition of increasing its presence there. He said Indian exporters have struggled to use the market access opportunities since the agreement was signed. Exports fell nearly 11% in 2025-26 and by over 9% in January to July 2026 over 2025, he said.
The Commerce Ministry said in May that India's exports to Switzerland, its largest EFTA partner, crossed $1.2 billion in 2025-26.
Products that overlap
India's exports to EFTA in 2024-25 included engineering goods worth $315 million, up 18% from the year before, according to the PIB. Dhar said telephones and electronics products, and textiles and clothing, have been among Vietnam's major exports to EFTA in recent years, and that India has considerable competitive strengths in these industries.
The European Union angle
EU-Vietnam goods trade was EUR 76 billion in 2025, and the EU's deficit was EUR 51.7 billion, according to the Commission. Machinery and appliances made up more than half of EU imports from Vietnam, followed by footwear and textiles.
On September 11, the Commission sent proposals to the EU Council seeking authorisation to sign and conclude the India deal.
India's Commerce Ministry put India's goods exports to the EU at $75.85 billion in 2024-25. It said $33 billion of India's labour-intensive exports, including textiles and leather and footwear, face EU duties of 4% to 26% and will move to zero at entry into force. It valued India's textile and apparel exports to the EU at $7.2 billion.
The $100 billion investment goal
Under Article 7.1(3) of TEPA, the EFTA states "shall aim to increase" foreign direct investment into India by $50 billion within 10 years of the agreement taking effect, and by another $50 billion in the following five years, according to the agreement text.

The PIB describes the commitments as binding. Under Article 7.7, a sub-committee will review progress at five, 10 and 15 years. If the objectives are not met by the final review, India can seek consultations and, if they fail, take temporary measures to rebalance its tariff concessions, the text says.
Srivastava described the commitment as "just an aspirational target tied to India's high GDP growth and high returns to EFTA companies in India." Dhar said: "These are still early days to assess whether there has been any forward movement on this promise."

articles.title: China keeps its benchmark lending rate unchanged for the 17th consecutive month: Prioritizing stable growth. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: China keeps its benchmark lending rate unchanged for the 17th consecutive month: Prioritizing stable growth.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
This signal reflects the world's most populous country's preference for stability in economic management without disrupting its financial markets. 
|  | 
| Maintaining the benchmark lending rate is a priority for stability in China 's economic management. (Image: East Asia Forum) | 
 The People's Bank of China has decided to keep the one-year loan prime rate (LPR) at 3% and the five-year rate at 3.5%. The one-year LPR is a key benchmark for business and household loans, while the five-year LPR significantly impacts home loan interest rates.
 Maintaining these two interest rate levels suggests that the central bank is not in a hurry to implement another round of monetary easing, especially after better-than-expected third-quarter growth figures.
 This decision aligns with expert forecasts and reflects the cautious approach of the authorities amidst signs of stabilization in the Chinese economy. China's gross domestic product (GDP) is projected to grow by 4.5% in the third quarter of 2026, higher than the 4.3% growth in the second quarter of 2026.
 These results help ease the pressure to immediately implement further monetary stimulus measures to achieve the annual growth target of 4.5% to 5%.
 However, the positive growth rate is not enough to erase the imbalances in the economy. Exports and manufacturing continue to play a crucial role, while domestic consumer demand remains weak, private investment lacks momentum, and the real estate market has yet to recover from its difficulties.
 This necessitates maintaining growth while limiting the risk of resources continuing to be concentrated in sectors with high production capacity but lacking corresponding demand.
 In this context, maintaining interest rate stability does not mean China is shrinking its role in monetary policy. On the contrary, it could allow the People's Bank of China to focus more on how credit is priced, allocated, and transmitted to the economy, rather than simply relying on raising or lowering the benchmark interest rate.
 One notable direction is the People's Bank of China's consideration of shifting the focus of its policy interest rate toward the overnight reverse lending rate, thereby gradually reducing its reliance on the current LPR mechanism.
 Governor Pan Gongsheng of the People's Bank of China said the central bank will aim to diversify benchmark interest rates in lending operations.
 According to the proposed scheme, financially sound businesses can choose the overnight reverse lending rate (LPR) as the basis for calculating interest on floating-rate loans. The overnight rate can also be used as a benchmark for bonds and financial derivatives.
 Essentially, this change aims towards a more flexible capital pricing system, where interest rates more closely reflect market conditions and the characteristics of each customer group.
 If implemented effectively, the new mechanism could help improve the transmission of monetary policy while providing businesses with more options in managing borrowing costs. Importantly, the transition does not necessarily have to happen simultaneously across the board.
 Expanding interest rate options, initially for financially sound businesses, can help the banking system and capital markets gradually adapt to the new mechanism. This approach also helps limit the risk of disruption to existing credit agreements, asset valuation practices, and business borrowing decisions.
 However, it must be acknowledged that diversifying benchmark interest rates does not automatically guarantee that credit will be allocated more efficiently. The greater challenge is ensuring that capital flows serve the intended growth objectives.
 It must also be said that not all problems can be solved by monetary policy alone. China is currently facing difficulties in the real estate market, cautious spending habits, and weakening private investment, all of which are related to income prospects, asset prices, profit expectations, and confidence in the business environment. These will be challenges that need continued attention in the coming period.
 Clearly, maintaining the LPR for the 17th consecutive month reflects China's preference for stability in its economic management. While growth hasn't lost momentum, domestic drivers remain weak, widespread monetary easing may not be the optimal solution.
 Maintaining stable interest rates at this stage therefore creates policy space for China to gradually adjust its credit pricing and allocation mechanisms, aiming to both maintain growth and limit unnecessary disruptions to the market and the economy.
