articles.title: Thailand's real estate growth shifts beyond Bangkok - DataCenterNews Asia Pacific
articles.summary: Thailand's real estate growth shifts beyond Bangkok  DataCenterNews Asia Pacific
articles.full_text:
JLL has identified Thailand as well placed to benefit from structural shifts in Southeast Asia's real estate market, with growth extending beyond Bangkok into industrial and tourism-linked regions.
Thailand's Eastern Economic Corridor remains the main anchor of expansion, but investment activity is also spreading to second-tier cities and coastal destinations. JLL also pointed to a broader regional pattern in which infrastructure investment, supply chain diversification, digitalisation and tighter sustainability standards are reshaping where capital is directed.
Thailand's changing real estate map reflects a shift away from a model concentrated on the capital. Growth is becoming more distributed, with the Eastern Seaboard, industrial townships and tourism-focused areas taking a larger share of development.
Part of that shift is tied to industrial policy and manufacturing trends. Thailand is moving further into higher-value industrial segments such as electronics, electric vehicles, specialised manufacturing and advanced logistics, as companies adjust supply chains under so-called China+1 strategies.
This is changing the nature of industrial property demand. Managed industrial parks and sector-specific clusters are gaining importance over more traditional land banking and warehouse-led approaches, particularly in areas linked to the Eastern Economic Corridor and the U-Tapao aviation hub.
Industrial focus
The findings place Thailand alongside other Southeast Asian markets where governments are using policy and infrastructure to shape investment patterns. Across the region, transport links, special economic zones and other state-led initiatives are widening the range of locations considered investable beyond traditional central business districts.
In Thailand, this has created what JLL describes as a more networked pattern of growth. The report identifies the Eastern Economic Corridor as one of several connected regional growth systems in Southeast Asia, alongside the Johor-Singapore axis, Northern Luzon and Vietnam's large regional clusters.
Industrial and logistics assets are one of four cross-cutting themes identified for investors and occupiers in Thailand. The others are data centres and digital infrastructure, asset repositioning and conversion, and cross-border corridor opportunities.
Bangkok remains central to the office and retail story, but the focus there is different. Rather than new development alone, ageing stock in the capital offers scope for retrofit, conversion and repositioning as occupiers place greater weight on building quality and environmental standards.
Rising ESG expectations are widening the gap between modern assets and outdated buildings. That is contributing to a broader "brown discount" for properties that are poorly configured, energy-inefficient or functionally obsolete.
Tourism markets
Outside the capital, JLL highlighted opportunities in hospitality, retail and residential projects linked to tourism and wellness. Phuket was described as an established global resort destination, while Phang Nga was identified as an emerging coastal market.
Wellness-led development is expected to play a bigger role in tourist-driven locations, especially across retail, ultra-luxury residential and hospitality segments. The report also noted that larger developers in Thailand are shifting towards recurring-income assets, contributing to a more diversified development pipeline.
Krit Pimhataivoot, Country Head & Head of Capital Markets, JLL Thailand, said the market was becoming more selective as investors and occupiers focused more tightly on fundamentals.
"Thailand's real estate market is moving into a more selective phase, where success depends on focusing on strong fundamentals. While policy and infrastructure remain key drivers, capital is deploying into highly specialised areas. We see this in the sustained demand for advanced industrial estates, the robust expansion of world-class tourism, hotel, and wellness developments in premier coastal destinations, and, in Bangkok, the practical opportunity of converting and upgrading existing office buildings to meet modern demands," said Pimhataivoot.
Regional shift
The wider Southeast Asian context is a key part of the assessment. JLL argues the region's outlook should be viewed less through a cyclical recovery lens and more through structural forces reshaping geography, asset selection and sector priorities.
That means broad exposure to a country or region may matter less than specific positions within growth corridors, sectors and asset types. In Thailand, the report suggests the strongest interest is likely to cluster around advanced industrial estates, tourism-linked destinations and urban assets that can be upgraded for new uses.
Dr Yang Liang Chua, Head of Research & Advisory, Southeast Asia, JLL, said Thailand reflects a wider regional shift towards more distributed growth.
"Thailand is a prime example of the regional expansion occurring across Southeast Asia, shifting from a Bangkok-focused market to a highly diversified, multipolar landscape. Investors are capitalizing on specialized opportunities across different regions, from advanced industrial estates in the Eastern Economic Corridor to premier, self-sustaining luxury hospitality and wellness markets in Phuket and upcoming coastal locations like Phang Nga," said Chua.
He added that Thailand should be viewed within a broader regional framework rather than as a single-city market.
"For investors and occupiers alike, Thailand offers compelling upside, particularly for those who approach it as part of a connected, multipolar system," he said.

articles.full_text:
Perikatan Nasional's dissolution would mean that its component parties would not be able to contest the upcoming elections under a common banner.
KUALA LUMPUR: Malaysia cancelled the registration of the country's main opposition coalition Perikatan Nasional (PN) on Tuesday (Oct 20) amid a dispute between its key parties, dealing a blow to the bloc ahead of elections expected in coming months.
Malaysia's Melaka state is due to hold a vote on Nov 14, in the latest test for Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim following defeats in two other regional polls earlier this year. An early general election could also be triggered amid simmering tensions within Anwar's multi-party ruling coalition.
But opposition group PN is facing growing rifts of its own between the conservative Islamist party Parti Islam Se-Malaysia (PAS) - which has the most seats of any single party in Malaysia's 222-member parliament - and the Malay nationalist party Parti Pribumi Bersatu Malaysia (Bersatu), with both vying for leadership of the coalition.
Bersatu, led by former prime minister Muhyiddin Yassin, had filed a complaint to the Registrar of Societies (RoS) alleging that it had been excluded from a PN supreme council meeting in July, describing it as a breach of the coalition's constitution by rival grouping PAS.
RoS said in a Tuesday statement that it had received an unsatisfactory response from PN after warning last month that the bloc could face de-registration.
It said "the reasons given failed to refute the grounds for the cancellation of registration".
PN's dissolution would mean that its component parties, including several other smaller organisations aside from Bersatu and PAS, would not be able to contest the elections under a common banner.
Despite contesting under the PN banner, Bersatu and PAS campaigned in the Johor and Negeri Sembilan state polls separately.
PN secretary-general Takiyuddin Hassan, who is also a PAS leader, said on Tuesday that the coalition would file a legal challenge against the de-registration order.
"PN condemns this action as an attempt to ... weaken political opponents ahead of the Melaka election," Takiyuddin said in a statement.
He said the RoS issued its show-cause notice on Sep 22, the day the dissolution of the Melaka state assembly was announced, and suspended PN’s activities the following day, local news outlet Free Malaysia Today reported.
Political parties under the now deregistered coalition have yet to decide which logo to use for the upcoming Melaka state polls, The Star reported Takiyuddinas saying.
Polling for the Melaka state election is scheduled for Nov 14, with nomination day on Oct 31 and early voting on Nov 10.
Anwar leads a government consisting of several blocs, including his own Pakatan Harapan coalition as well as the Barisan Nasional (BN), led by the once-dominant United Malays National Organisation (UMNO), the party of jailed former premier Najib Razak.
Despite their federal partnership, Pakatan and Barisan remain rivals in some states, with the parties exploring different electoral strategies ahead of the next general election.
BN and PAS have said they are discussing cooperation in the Melaka polls, an arrangement that could test the prospects of a broader electoral alliance, according to local media reports.

articles.title: A football meme sparked boycott calls for an Indonesian grooming brand. What can be learnt from Kahf’s misstep? - CNA
articles.summary: A football meme sparked boycott calls for an Indonesian grooming brand. What can be learnt from Kahf’s misstep?  CNA
articles.full_text:
Kahf has faced boycott calls in Malaysia after a football meme was perceived as belittling the country and other regional neighbours.
KUALA LUMPUR: A men’s grooming brand from Indonesia has faced widespread boycott calls from Malaysian consumers, with many taking to social media to air their grievances.
The cause: A football-themed meme from the grooming label Kahf that appeared to disparage other countries after Indonesia won a regional tournament.
The reaction was swift. Across social media platforms including Threads, Facebook, and TikTok, disgruntled Malaysian consumers are sharing videos of themselves discarding Kahf products into trash bins, urging fellow citizens to shun the brand, which is sold online and in big pharmacy chains.
The backlash has quickly metastasised into a broader campaign targeting ParagonCorp’s - Kahf’s parent company - wider consumer portfolio, such as its sister brand Wardah. The latter is a popular halal-certified cosmetics and skincare brand.
Some have even called for broader boycotts of Indonesian brands in Malaysia, though this has not gained as much traction.
The episode underscores the risks brands face as they expand across Southeast Asia, experts told CNA, where attempts to engage consumers through informal online banter can quickly backfire when they collide with national pride and cultural sensitivities.
WHAT LED TO THIS BOYCOTT?
The issue began after Indonesia beat Thailand to win the inaugural FIFA ASEAN Cup on home soil at Gelora Bung Karno Stadium in Jakarta on Oct 5. Kahf shared a meme on its Threads account with the words “hati-hati beda level”. It translates to “be careful, different levels”.
The words separated the Indonesian flag above that of other countries, including Malaysia, Singapore and Thailand.
Kahf removed the post and issued a public apology, saying that it was unacceptable and did not “reflect our values and the respect we stand for as a brand”.
“The bond between Malaysian and Indonesian communities has always been rooted in brotherhood and respect. We are committed to upholding the same respect across all countries and cultures. We take full responsibility for falling short of that commitment,” it said on its Threads account on Oct 7, two days after the initial post went out.
“Thank you for holding us accountable. We understand that rebuilding trust takes more than an apology. We are committed to earning it back through our actions.”
But the post did little to quell the anger, with Malaysian social media users continuing to call for a boycott of the brand.
“Being three years loyal customer, and all it took was one post for you to destroy your own reputation,” Threads user dzack_ko said in a comment on Kahf’s post on Oct 10, accompanied by a video of him throwing Kahf products into the trash.
Another Threads user, Dora.mr5, said that there was no need for the brand to put Malaysia down.
“Kahf can succeed through its own efforts, but don't let that make you feel so superior that you insult another country … Competition is normal, but manners and respect must always be maintained," read the comment.
Other users took a more retaliatory stance, mockingly quipping that Indonesia’s transboundary haze and poverty rates were the real things operating at "higher levels" - a potshot at the meme that the brand had posted and eventually deleted.
Oh Ei Sun, principal adviser at Pacific Research Center of Malaysia, told CNA that exchanges between Malaysia and Indonesian social media users can be particularly heated, with cross-border banter often spiralling into toxic discourse.
Oh said that the timing of the controversy coincided with heightened regional frustrations over the haze, as forest fires in Indonesia inundate neighbouring countries like Malaysia and Singapore with choking smog, forcing the shutdown of schools among other things.
"This is already a high-tension period," Oh said, adding that comments by certain Indonesian officials on the haze, for example, did not help the situation.
Indonesian Government Communications Agency chief Syahganda Nainggolan was reported to have said that the country’s forests provide the region’s oxygen, prompting Malaysian netizens to react with disbelief and sarcasm.
“We don’t just send smoke; when there is no smoke, we send oxygen,” he said in a widely circulated video published by Kompas, an Indonesian media outlet. “The oxygen in Singapore and Malaysia also comes from our forests.”
Oh recalled his own brush with “digital nationalism” after commenting online about the accidental upside-down printing of the Indonesian flag during the 2017 Southeast Asian (SEA) Games in Kuala Lumpur.
Oh said his post attracted about 4,000 hostile comments from Indonesian social media users within an hour, prompting him to temporarily deactivate his account.
Taking a more forgiving stance, Malaysian Muay Thai fighter and Kahf brand ambassador Johan Ghazali acknowledged the company's misstep but urged consumers to move forward following its public apology.
“As long as we apologise, we can move on. It really isn’t that big of a deal, chill guys,” said Johan on his Threads page on Oct 7. He competes in the Flyweight division of the ONE Championship.
Many netizens criticised the fighter for dismissing the issue and drew comparisons to actor and singer Alif Satar - another Kahf ambassador in Malaysia - who was seen to have taken a firmer stance.
Alif had said that while he noted Kahf's apology, trust had to be restored through clear, concrete actions.
“I hope this matter can be resolved amicably, maturely, and with mutual respect. I believe that, under any circumstances, we can hold differing views without needing to put anyone down," he said in a Threads post on Oct 8.
WHY IS THIS A PROBLEM FOR SOUTHEAST ASIAN BRANDS?
For regional brands like Kahf, market expansion beyond Indonesia is essential for sustained growth. In Malaysia, the brand has built a presence through targeted lifestyle marketing, sports event sponsorships, lifestyle gatherings and high-profile brand collaborations.
But as brands try to stay culturally relevant across multiple markets, blending localised banter with communications can also alienate consumers across national borders.
Benjamin Loh, a media and communications lecturer at Monash University Malaysia, said brands are increasingly adopting informal, “netizen-like banter” to drive public engagement. But he warned against overindulging in this type of discourse.
“As brands make themselves more ‘human’, then similarly it invites more attacks against them. It's not the easiest line to straddle as insult-based banter will always end up insulting potential customers,” he said.
Loh added that social media has made social movements, including boycotts, much easier to organise and execute.
In Kahf’s case, the backlash has prompted calls on social media for Malaysians to boycott the brand and switch to home-grown grooming and personal care products instead.
Kahf is not the first brand to face consumer pushback in Southeast Asia, with similar controversies in recent years fuelled by geopolitical tensions.
Chinese tea chain Chagee faced boycott calls in Malaysia and Vietnam last year over depictions of the South China Sea on its mobile app, while Thai coffee chain Cafe Amazon faced a backlash in Cambodia amid diplomatic tensions between the two countries.
Beyond regional spats, Malaysian consumers have also participated in broader economic boycotts, like the global Boycott, Divestment, Sanctions (BDS) campaign targeting corporations perceived to have links to Israel.
In commenting on the Kahf issue, Threads user eafa_fiza said Malaysians should realise their purchasing power can have an impact on a firm’s bottom line.
“We decide who stays and who shuts down. This shows how strong we are when we unite. One silent boycott and a global brand can lose RM292 million (US$71.5 million) and close 88 stores. The power is truly in the hands of the consumers,” she wrote, referring to Starbucks in Malaysia, which has faced boycott calls over its perceived links to Israel amid the Israel-Hamas war.
According to a Bloomberg report, Starbucks operator Berjaya Food Bhd recorded an annual net loss of RM292 million in June 2025. The company cited the sustained fallout from Middle East conflict-related consumer sentiment, which disrupted market dynamics and shifted local spending patterns.
Sunway University economist Yeah Kim Leng told CNA that while social media boycotts trigger short-term sales dips and nationalist sentiment, they rarely inflict permanent brand damage.
"Eventually, product functionality prevails over emotion once rationality returns. Unless alternatives offer equal or better value, consumer sentiment usually gives way to product functionality once emotions cool down and rational purchasing habits return,” he said.
Yeah added that unlike short-lived social media disputes, campaigns like the BDS movement are far more enduring because they resonate across broader segments of society and tap into deeper ideological convictions.
Indonesia’s Trade Minister Budi Santoso was reported to have downplayed the boycott calls of Indonesian products and brands, saying that it had not affected bilateral trade relations between the two countries.
"I don't think it has (an impact). This is probably just a temporary response," Budi was quoted as saying by local news outlet Tempo on Oct 8.
WHAT BRANDS HAVE TO DO ONLINE
Ultimately, experts say that brands have to be more careful about what they post online.
Syed Mohammed Idid, the deputy chairman of the Public Relations Practitioners Society of Malaysia, told CNA that regional brands must treat cultural sensitivity and public sentiment as an absolute priority.

articles.title: How to Improve Global Mineral Governance - Cambodianess
articles.summary: How to Improve Global Mineral Governance  Cambodianess
articles.full_text:
- 
                                    By:
                                    
                                    
                                
- Hasrul Hanif
- October 21, 2026, 8:15 PM
The race to secure critical minerals has intensified at the same time as the international community has recognized the need for more sustainable and responsible mining practices. Translating the resulting frameworks and guidelines into concrete action will require consolidating Global South policy and advocacy networks.
OGYAKARTA—Interdependence may be the theme of this year’s annual meeting of the Intergovernmental Forum on Mining, Minerals, Metals, and Sustainable Development (IGF), held in Geneva on October 12–14, but competition between countries to secure transition minerals remains intense. This scramble could have dire consequences for mineral-producing countries if it undermines sustainability standards and prevents equitable cost- and benefit-sharing between and within countries.
The International Energy Agency estimates that, to achieve net-zero emissions, demand for critical minerals will triple by 2030 and quadruple by 2040. Mineral-rich countries, aware of the “resource curse,” are seeking ways to retain control over their reserves. In a bid to promote domestic value addition and meet their economic-development objectives, many of these countries are pursuing export bans on critical raw materials.
But Indonesia’s experience as one of the first countries to implement such a ban shows that downstream industrialization is not a cure-all. It can come with substantial environmental and social costs, and the benefits are not always shared equitably with the local communities that often bear the greatest burden of extraction and processing. And while extraction, smelting, and processing have boosted economic growth in Indonesia’s three nickel-rich provinces, they have not contributed significantly to the national economy. Frontier-making—the act of transforming marginal areas into centers of resource extraction—can create new “sacrifice zones” when not accompanied by robust regulation and democratic oversight.
Meanwhile, the emphasis on sustainable mining has never been greater at the global level. In 2024, the United Nations Secretary-General’s Panel on Critical Energy Transition Minerals released a set of guiding principles that underscore the need for a new paradigm rooted in justice and equity, and for mining to benefit host countries and local communities. Regional frameworks, including the African Union’s Africa Mining Vision, its follow-up guidelines and frameworks, and the ASEAN Principles for Sustainable Minerals Development, reflect similar commitments.
These agreements are sidelined, however, when countries pursue bilateral agreements that prioritize market access over all else. Consider the uneven treatment of nickel and palm oil in the EU–Indonesia Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement. The European Union has strict sustainability standards for palm oil, but not for nickel, even though both sectors can cause significant social and environmental degradation.
The best way to put principles into practice is to consolidate Global South policy and advocacy networks. This would enable policymakers, civil society, and local communities to share their experience with mineral extraction and processing and their proposals for making the sector more equitable and environmentally responsible.
There is a genuine desire among policymakers in the Global South to share the lessons learned from their successes and failures. The Natural Resource Governance Institute’s South–South Transition Minerals Learning Platform has facilitated the dissemination of policy insights among government officials from Indonesia, Chile, Zambia, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and other countries. While they share the same goal—to build more inclusive, resilient, and prosperous societies using mineral wealth—the platform enables a deeper understanding of how variations in commodities, domestic political economies, and value-chain positions require different strategies, rather than a one-size-fits-all approach.
Equally important are transnational or transcalar advocacy networks that connect civil-society groups across the Global South. They, too, can provide a platform for sharing experience and knowledge, while also strengthening collective action and extending accountability beyond national borders. By producing wide-ranging evidence of social and environmental abuses linked to mineral extraction, smelting, and processing, domestic advocacy actors can bypass governments and companies that do not adequately support local communities and directly seek out international allies to apply outside pressure.
Here, again, Indonesia provides a useful example. The prominent Indonesian NGO WALHI, together with Friends of the Earth Japan, mobilized more than one hundred organizations to urge Vale Indonesia’s shareholders to act on alleged human-rights abuses at the Sorowako nickel project. Some shareholders, including Vale, Sumitomo Metal Mining, and Mitsui & Co., responded by exerting pressure on the company when the government failed to do so effectively.
Similarly, campaigners from Mighty Earth, Climate Rights International, and Global Witness attracted investors’ attention by alleging widespread abuses in Indonesia’s nickel extraction and processing industry. They urged electric-vehicle battery and car producers to comply with social and environmental standards and due-diligence obligations. Weda Bay Nickel has since expressed interest in complying with Initiative for Responsible Mining Assurance standards, and some automakers have imposed stricter requirements on nickel suppliers.
This global pressure—which includes Publish What You Pay Indonesia raising concerns about the country’s nickel governance at the 2025 OECD Forum on Responsible Mineral Supply Chains—has forced the Indonesian government’s hand. After assessing the gap between its regulatory framework and three global standards, the government is preparing ESG (environmental, social, and governance) guidelines to help firms identify which Indonesian regulations meet the requirements of global standards in the nickel supply chain.
Advancing inclusion in transition-mineral supply chains—the goal of the IGF meeting—requires strategies for translating lofty declarations into concrete action. This can be achieved by bringing together and strengthening Global South policy and advocacy networks. Existing South–South cooperation mechanisms can expand their reach to facilitate policy learning on critical minerals, while domestic civil-society groups can deepen their global connections to put a spotlight on mining-related environmental destruction and human-rights abuses. Many pieces of the puzzle are already in place; now it is time to put them together.
Hasrul Hanif is Assistant Professor of Energy Politics at Universitas Gadjah Mada.
The article first appeared on the Project Syndicate.

Hong Kong (VNA) – Vietnam has announced four priority topics for the APEC Finance Ministers’ Process 2027, focusing on capital markets, data-driven finance, development financing and young talent in the financial sector.
In an interview with Vietnam News Agency correspondents in Hong Kong (China) on October 21, following the conclusion of the 33rd APEC Finance Ministers’ Meeting, Minister of Finance Ngo Van Tuan highlighted the meeting’s key outcomes, Vietnam’s economic performance and strategic orientations for APEC Year 2027, which Vietnam will host.
Assessing the meeting’s overall results, Tuan said the 2026 gathering achieved significant strategic and practical outcomes. Participating economies adopted a joint statement reaffirming their strong commitment to building an open, dynamic, resilient and peaceful Asia-Pacific community by 2040. They also reached broad consensus on maintaining flexible and credible fiscal and monetary policies to safeguard regional financial stability.
At the macroeconomic session, the Vietnamese representative delivered a keynote speech highlighting the country’s economic achievements. Vietnam’s GDP expanded by 9.01% in the first nine months of 2026, with growth reaching 9.95% in the third quarter.
Vietnam’s entry into the upper-middle-income country group, the upgrading of its stock market to emerging-market status and its first investment-grade rating from a reputable global credit rating agency have further strengthened the country’s international standing, the minister said.
A key highlight of the meeting was Vietnam’s official announcement of four priority topics for the APEC Finance Ministers’ Process in 2027, which it assumed the chairmanship of on October 21.
The priorities are strengthening capital markets to mobilise private capital for innovative businesses, promoting data-driven finance to improve access to capital for micro, small and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs), diversifying financial resources for development, and enhancing the capacity of young people in the financial sector.
Tuan stressed that these priorities were fully aligned with the Incheon Plan for 2026–2030 and Vietnam’s major development orientations.
Discussions on these topics are expected to help refine domestic financial mechanisms and policies in support of the Party and State’s development agenda for 2026–2030. They are closely tied to major Politburo resolutions, such as Resolution No. 57-NQ/TW on breakthroughs in science and technology, innovation, and national digital transformation; Resolution No. 59-NQ/TW on international integration in the new context; and Resolution No. 68-NQ/TW on promoting private-sector growth.
The priorities also align with Vietnam’s Financial Strategy to 2030 and the country’s development goals for 2026–2030, as well as its vision towards 2045, as outlined in documents of the 14th National Party Congress.
On the sidelines of the meeting, the Vietnamese Ministry of Finance delegation held a series of bilateral meetings with key partners, including those from China, the US, Thailand, and the World Bank.
International partners expressed strong support and pledged close cooperation with the ministry, laying a solid foundation for the successful hosting of APEC Year 2027./.

articles.title: Thai Banks' Q3 Profits Diverge Amid Margin Squeeze as Fee Income Offsets - Nation Thailand
articles.summary: Thai Banks' Q3 Profits Diverge Amid Margin Squeeze as Fee Income Offsets  Nation Thailand
articles.full_text:
Six lenders offset weaker interest income with wealth and insurance fees and tight cost control, while bolstering reserves against flood risks.
Thailand's six listed banks reported mixed third-quarter results this week. Falling interest rates squeezed lending income, and the lenders relied on fee income, cost discipline and prudent provisioning to protect earnings.
Combined nine-month net profit across Bangkok Bank, Kasikornbank (KBank), SCB X (SCBX), Krungsri, TMBThanachart (ttb) and Kiatnakin Phatra (KKP) came to about 150.8bn baht, according to the banks' disclosures.
This total is our own tally, and reporting bases differ between banks.
Three banks reported higher profits year on year, led by KKP. Bangkok Bank and SCBX reported declines, and ttb did not give a comparison.
The banks described an uneven economy. Exports, particularly electronics tied to the global artificial intelligence (AI) cycle, and large corporates remain strong.
Households and small businesses are under pressure from high debt and living costs, and tourism is recovering more slowly than expected. Flooding late in the quarter added to the strain, while limited government finances constrain further stimulus.
Lenders cut rates to ease customers' burdens, which hit net interest income. Most banks grew loans selectively, favouring large corporate, digital and overseas lending over domestic SME and retail segments.
All six reported capital ratios comfortably above regulatory minimums. Several set aside extra "management overlay" provisions against flood damage and economic uncertainty.
Bangkok Bank earned 29.98bn baht in the first nine months, down from a year earlier. It cited lower net interest income after rate reductions and weaker investment gains. Net interest margin was 2.47 per cent. Fees rose on bancassurance, mutual funds and securities business.
Operating expenses fell 4.6 per cent, putting the cost-to-income ratio at 48.2 per cent, and expected credit losses fell 13.9 per cent. Loans rose 3.2 per cent from the end of 2025 to 2.69 trillion baht on large corporate and international lending.
Deposits rose 0.8 per cent to 3.22 trillion baht. The bad-loan ratio was 3.2 per cent, but coverage was 322.1 per cent, the highest among the six. The capital adequacy ratio was 21.5 per cent.
The bank described itself as a "trusted partner and reliable close friend" to customers. It backs the government's SMEs Credit Boost programme and says it will continue responsible lending. Its release did not name an executive.
KBank's third-quarter profit was 12.72bn baht, down 2.1 per cent year on year and 3.98 per cent from the previous quarter. Market volatility cut financial-instrument income, and net fees fell 5.29 per cent on market conditions and new fee-collection rules.
Nine-month profit rose 3.43 per cent to 40.64bn baht, helped by a one-off 1.46bn baht investment compensation. Excluding that item, profit was 39.31bn baht, close to last year's level.
Net interest income fell 8.87 per cent to 94.99bn baht, with a margin of 2.89 per cent. Non-interest income jumped 21.51 per cent to 51.89bn baht on wealth management, fund management and insurance.
The cost-to-income ratio was 40.79 per cent. Provisions of 30.17bn baht put credit cost at 1.60 per cent, the top of its 1.40–1.60 per cent target range. Coverage rose to 177.9 per cent.
Chief executive Khattiya Indaravijaya said the recovery remained "K-shaped", with government measures offering only partial support in the final quarter given budget limits. She warned that household purchasing power is fragile and that energy prices remain elevated because of Middle East uncertainty. The bank expects operating expenses to rise seasonally in the fourth quarter.
SCBX reported a third-quarter profit of 10.68bn baht, down 4.0 per cent quarter on quarter. Rising bond yields caused mark-to-market losses on debt holdings, leaving investment and trading income at a 424 million baht loss.
Nine-month profit was 31.99bn baht, down 14.3 per cent year on year. Core operations held up better. Net interest income edged up 0.5 per cent to 27.45bn baht, with net interest margin rising to 3.07 per cent.
Fee and other income rose 6.2 per cent year on year to 11.50bn baht, and nine-month growth of 12.8 per cent has already exceeded the full-year target. Operating costs fell 6.3 per cent year on year on AI and automation.
SCB Bank's bad-loan ratio improved for a sixth straight quarter to 2.95 per cent, though the group ratio edged up to 3.21 per cent on a planned portfolio adjustment at AutoX. Credit cost fell to 1.37 per cent, coverage was 159.4 per cent and the capital ratio was 18.5 per cent.
Chief executive Arthid Nanthawithaya said volatility had become "an enduring feature of the operating environment". He pointed to three priorities: quality growth, non-interest income and proactive asset-quality management.
The group is preparing to launch a virtual bank and is helping indebted customers through its "Khun Su, Rao Chuay" scheme. Arak Sutivong takes over as chief executive on 1 January 2027.
Krungsri's nine-month profit rose 3.9 per cent to 25.57bn baht, supported by corporate and ASEAN lending, the consolidation of consumer lender TIDLOR and lower funding costs. Its net interest margin improved to 4.58 per cent from 4.28 per cent, the highest of the six banks.
Loans rose 0.8 per cent to 1.94 trillion baht. Corporate and ASEAN portfolios grew 6.5 and 7.7 per cent respectively, offsetting declines in SME and domestic retail lending.
Deposits fell 1.7 per cent as the bank cut costly time deposits. Non-interest income rose 3.7 per cent and the cost-to-income ratio improved to 45.6 per cent.
The bad-loan ratio eased to 3.19 per cent, with coverage of 143.1 per cent, the lowest of the six, and credit cost of 231 basis points.
Chief executive Kenichi Yamato said Krungsri delivered "resilient performance" in a challenging backdrop. He expects a gradual recovery supported by private investment and technology exports and forecasts Thai GDP growth of 2.1 per cent for 2026.
ttb earned 5.46bn baht in the third quarter and 16.14bn baht in nine months. Nine-month operating income rose 3.3 per cent to 50.86bn baht, and pre-provision profit was flat at 27.52bn baht.
Nine-month operating expenses rose 7.2 per cent, but the cost-to-income ratio stayed on target at 46 per cent. Loans were 1.187 trillion baht, up 0.3 per cent on the quarter but down 1.5 per cent year to date.
Deposits rose 1.0 per cent year to date to 1.282 trillion baht. Provisions totalled 12.11bn baht for nine months, down 5.8 per cent. The bad-loan ratio fell to 2.88 per cent and coverage rose to 159 per cent from 152 per cent at the end of 2025. Capital adequacy was 18.8 per cent.
Chief executive Piti Tantakasem said results were in line with targets. The bank launched its "Tang Luk" flood-relief programme, running to 31 December, which it expects to cover under 1 per cent of loans.
It is building a wealth business with DBS Bank, Schroders and Webull and has 14 billion baht left in its share buyback. More than 86,200 customers have joined its debt-consolidation programme, which the bank says cuts interest costs by about 3.4 billiomn baht.
KKP was the standout performer. Third-quarter profit rose 43.0 per cent year on year to 2.39bn baht and nine-month profit climbed 56.1 per cent to 6.47bn baht.
Non-interest income rose 40.2 per cent over nine months, driven by wealth management, the Dime! investment platform, fund fees, investment banking and insurance brokerage.
Its securities arm retains the top share of brokerage trading. Net interest income rose 6.5 per cent in the quarter. Loans grew 3.7 per cent year to date. The bad-loan ratio fell to 3.4 per cent from 4.3 per cent at the end of 2025, and coverage rose to 154.7 per cent. Its release did not include a chief executive statement.
The banks' earnings drivers are shifting from lending margins to fees and wealth management. Cost control, helped by AI adoption, is a common theme.
Asset quality is stable and buffers are thick, but the banks flag the same risks: flood damage, stretched households and global volatility.
Executives expect the final quarter to be cautious, with rising seasonal costs at KBank and continued relief programmes at ttb and SCBX.

articles.full_text:

KUALA LUMPUR – Malaysia has banned its civil servants from using the Israel-linked navigation app Waze, citing security concerns over sensitive government information and personal data.
Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim also urged all citizens to stop using the app, reflecting a growing global push towards digital sovereignty as governments seek greater control over citizens’ data.
“Sensitive government information and the personal data of citizens must be protected from exploitation by the Israeli regime in ways that could undermine national security and sovereignty,” said a statement from the Prime Minister’s Office on Oct 21.
Anwar raised concerns that the data is governed by Waze Mobile, which was incorporated in Israel and operates under Israeli law.
He also urged Malaysians to stop using Waze and switch to locally developed alternatives such as TuJu, citing their purported data security and privacy protections.
The announcement came after Anwar chaired a meeting with the National Cyber Security Committee on Oct 20.
The Straits Times previously sighted a memo on the ban, which was issued to Malaysian civil servants by Chief Secretary to the Government Shamsul Azri Abu Bakar on Oct 20.
Founded in Israel in 2008 and acquired by US technology giant Google in 2013, the Waze app remains operated by Waze Mobile, which is based in Tel Aviv, according to its privacy policy.
Malaysia has long supported the Palestinian cause and refuses to recognise Israel diplomatically.
Global spyware fears fuel ban
The decision came days after researchers at the University of Toronto’s Citizen Lab and cybersecurity firm Confiant revealed that Israeli advertising company Discover-Tech allegedly exploited online advertisements to track internet users and facilitate spyware attacks.
Its ads appeared across more than 120,000 websites and 75,000 mobile apps, potentially exposing hundreds of millions of users to surveillance.
The researchers linked the operation to Israeli spyware developer Candiru, whose software was used to target 45 devices belonging to Qatar-based broadcaster Al Jazeera between 2024 and 2025.
Reuters also reported that the ads reached sensitive networks associated with NATO, the Pentagon and the United Nations, although there is no evidence that all these networks were compromised.
Munira Mustaffa, a security expert at Chasseur Group, said recent revelations about Israeli-linked surveillance operations targeting Al Jazeera through sophisticated, virtually undetectable online ads have heightened concerns around potential espionage.
“The Israeli situation presents serious concerns,” Munira said.
“For example, several European countries are actively seeking to reduce reliance on Microsoft after reports emerged that Unit 8200 utilised Microsoft’s cloud servers in the Netherlands and Ireland to store data on Palestinians targeted for surveillance.”
Unit 8200 refers to the Israeli military’s principal signals intelligence and cyberwarfare unit.
In January, France announced plans to phase out American video-conferencing services such as Zoom and Microsoft Teams across government agencies by 2027, while Germany and India have introduced their own messaging applications for public servants over security and data protection concerns.
Fitness-tracking app Strava has also raised security concerns after its publicly accessible Global Positioning System heatmaps exposed military bases and troop movements worldwide.
These include locations near Ukraine in 2018, potentially providing intelligence for enemy attacks.
In 2023, former Russian submarine commander Stanislav Rzhitsky was shot dead while jogging in Krasnodar, with Russian media speculating that his killer had tracked his movements through fitness app Strava, which showed he regularly ran along the route where he was killed.
However, it remains unclear whether the data was used to plan the assassination.
Historical military precedents for ban
The Malaysian Armed Forces had similarly raised concerns about location-based apps a decade earlier, when the augmented-reality mobile game Pokemon Go became a global phenomenon.
In August 2016, then Armed Forces chief Raja Mohamed Affandi Mohamed Noor warned that the game’s GPS-based features could compromise military camps, personnel and equipment.
Then Defence Minister Hishammuddin Hussein subsequently ordered restrictions on Pokemon Go around sensitive military installations, warning that it could be exploited to obtain images of locations not visible through Google Earth.
Farlina Said, a cybersecurity expert at the Institute of Strategic and International Studies Malaysia, said that in some countries where data security for those in the public sector is higher, apps that can access location should not be used unless approved or verified.
“In Malaysia’s case, it may be the uncertainty of means and location where data is being processed which can raise distrust towards such applications,” Farlina told ST.
However, TuJu, the navigation app promoted by Anwar and developed by the Malaysian Highway Authority, has had a rocky start, with users complaining about software crashes, inaccurate information and missing features.
Among the complaints are the lack of support for in-car infotainment systems and inaccurate speed readings. These include instances of the app displaying vehicles travelling at negative speeds.
“The shout-out for TuJu is understandable considering the circumstances, but the app’s a long way off from being dependable for most Malaysians,” user Ganaesh Devaraj wrote on Threads.

| The Landmark 81 building in HCM City, which was developed by Vingroup. Shares of the conglomerate logged the biggest daily gain of 7 per cent on Wednesday, leading the market's bullish trend. — Photo vingroup.net | 
HÀ NỘI — The market increased strongly on Wednesday, with the VN-Index breaking above the 1,700-point threshold, as buying spread across the market, particularly in real estate and securities stocks.
On the Hochiminh Stock Exchange (HoSE), the VN-Index surged 46.7 points, or 2.76 per cent, to 1,738.67 points. In terms of percentage gain, it was the benchmark' strongest session in six months.
The breadth of the market was positive, as the number of the gainers surpassed that of the decliners by three times. Liquidity also increased from the previous session to more than VNĐ20.2 trillion (US$784 million).
The 30 biggest stocks tracker, VN30-Index, jumped 35.06 points, or 1.9 per cent, to 1,880.57 points. Up to 25 stocks in the VN30 basket ticked up, while only one ended lower and four stayed flat.
Similarly, the HNX-Index on the Hanoi Stock Exchange (HNX) rose 3.71 points, or 1.44 per cent, to 261.67 points.
Large-cap stocks provided the main impetus for the rally, particularly those linked to Vingroup. Of which, Vingroup (VIC), Vinhomes (VHM) and Vincom Retail (VRE) all hit daily ceiling prices.
VIC contributed 23.37 points to the VN-Index, while VHM added 6.78 points, making the two stocks the leading contributors to the benchmark's advance.
Buying momentum also extended beyond the largest property stocks. Bluemarq Group (DXG) climbed 6.94 per cent, Nam Long Group (NLG) rose 6.78 per cent, Phat Dat Real Estate Development Corporation (PDR) advanced 5.73 per cent, VPI gained 5.46 per cent, CEO Group (CEO) increased 5.45 per cent and Khang Dien House (KDH) added 4.95 per cent.
Banking and securities stocks also supported the market's recovery.
In the banking sector, TPBank (TPB) rose 5.42 per cent, Vietinbank (CTG) gained 4.16 per cent, LPBank (LPB) advanced 4.89 per cent, Maritime Bank (MSB) increased 3.67 per cent, VIB climbed 2.55 per cent and Sahabank (SHB) added 2.37 per cent.
Foreign investors also returned to net buying on the southern market, snapping its net selling streak of 20 sessions. Particularly, they net bought VNĐ193 billion worth of shares on HoSE.

articles.title: Why China’s New Military Facility in Laos Matters - The China-Global South Project
articles.summary: Why China’s New Military Facility in Laos Matters  The China-Global South Project

China’s new joint air training facility in Laos highlights Beijing’s incremental expansion of its military access across Southeast Asia. The 2,000-meter runway could extend the operational reach of Chinese aircraft, although its current capabilities remain limited and its long-term purpose is uncertain. Unlike a conventional overseas base, the facility reflects a gradual approach to expanding China’s regional security footprint.
The bigger story may be Beijing’s deepening political and economic influence in Laos, where Chinese investment, debt exposure, and growing party-to-party ties strengthen bilateral relations. As Japan expands security cooperation across Southeast Asia and the United States maintains its regional military presence, China’s evolving access arrangements could gradually reshape the regional balance of power.
Hunter Marston, director of the Southeast Asia Program at the Lowy Institute and project lead for the Asia Power Index, joins Eric to talk about China’s military ambitions in Laos, the strategic implications of its growing regional access, and the roles of economic leverage and Japan’s expanding security partnerships.

📌 Topics Covered in This Episode
- China’s New Air Training Facility in Laos
- Beijing’s Growing Political and Economic Influence in Laos
- China’s Military Access and Southeast Asian Security
- Japan’s Expanding Security Role in the Indo-Pacific
About Hunter Marston:
Dr. Hunter Marston is the Director of the Southeast Asia Program at the Lowy Institute and Project Lead for the Asia Power Index. His research focuses on great power competition in Southeast Asia, Indo-Pacific security and alliances, and U.S. foreign policy, with particular attention to the evolving strategic dynamics shaping the region.
Marston is also an Adjunct Nonresident Fellow with the Center for Strategic and International Studies’ Southeast Asia Program, an Adjunct Research Fellow at La Trobe Asia, and an Associate with 9DashLine. He holds a PhD in International Relations from the Australian National University, a master’s degree in Southeast Asian Studies, and a Master of Public Administration from the University of Washington.
Previously, Marston worked with the Brookings Institution’s Center for East Asia Policy Studies and the Center for Strategic and International Studies. His analysis and commentary have appeared in Foreign Affairs, Foreign Policy, The New York Times, The Washington Post, and other leading academic and international publications.

Every year, the Pentagon submits a report to Congress on its assessment of the PLA, and every year they include a long list of countries that China is purportedly considering where it wants to build some military outpost. We’ve talked a lot on this show about how much of that rhetoric coming out of the Pentagon is just sheer fantasy, and how it’s a little odd that a country with more than 800 bases around the world is concerned about a rival that up until recently just had one.
Well, China’s overseas count has gone up recently, and it’s now somewhere between one and three.
There’s the base in Djibouti, which by the conventional definition is a proper military base. Then there’s a joint Cambodian naval facility at the Ream Naval Base. Calling that facility, calling the PLA’s operations there a base, is probably overstating it, but they definitely have an ongoing presence there.
And then we learned a few weeks ago that the PLA Air Force built a joint military support and training facility at the Bangun airport in Laos, near the Thai border. Now, we don’t know much about the facility, but satellite images have revealed a few clues. There’s a 2,000-meter-long runway with parking spaces for roughly two dozen aircraft.
So far, we haven’t seen any of China’s advanced fighter jets like the J-10s or the JF-16s. Instead, what we see from the satellite pictures are JL-8 trainer and light attack jets that are used by both the Chinese and the Laotians. But again, none of China’s more sophisticated fighter jets and certainly none of the larger jets that are probably not compatible with that airstrip.
China, for its part, denies that it’s a formal Air Force base and instead insists that the facility is intended to train Lao Air Force pilots and foster closer security cooperation with its southern neighbor. Well, let’s find out more from someone who’s been following this story very closely. Hunter Marston is the director of the Southeast Asia Program at the Lowy Institute, and project lead for the Asia Power Index.
Shortly after the base in Laos was announced, he wrote a fascinating article for The Interpreter, What to Make of China’s New Air Facility in Laos. And he joins us today to help us all figure it out. Hunter, good afternoon to you and thanks so much for joining us.
HUNTER MARSTON: Good afternoon, Eric. Thank you very much for having me on the show.
ERIC OLANDER: Let’s start with what this thing is. Is it a base? Is it a training center? What do you make of it?

But the air center seems more generally to be just infrastructure with potential to grow in the future at this point. And the longer-term implications of it remain uncertain at this point.

So it doesn’t seem to be an exclusive Chinese base. Cambodia’s politics have shifted somewhat in the last decade. And the Trump and Biden administrations before it have both invested considerable attention in pulling Phnom Penh away from the Chinese orbit.
And I think the leadership in Phnom Penh also recognizes that too much reliance on China potentially exposes them to coercion and unwanted leverage or intervention from Beijing. So Cambodia’s politics have shifted to an extent that I think makes it less attractive to seek to take advantage of and form or put new bases in. Laos, on the other hand, is relatively open to Chinese investment and infrastructure.
The political ties between the Lao Revolutionary Party and the Communist Party of China are significant and growing. And I think Laos is seen as the natural partner for such a new endeavor for China’s military expansion in Southeast Asia. It also positions China’s operations and gives it extended range further southwest, potentially allowing it to reach the Indian Ocean.
Now, again, we don’t know the long-term usage of the Ban Keun air facility. So it could be that China is using it for training, using it to support its own multilateral or bilateral military exercises with other Southeast Asian countries. But it also allows the prepositioning of certain assets that would allow it to reach more easily the Indian Ocean and further into South Asia. So that’s where I’d keep my eye in the future.

articles.summary: Bond issuance slows, interest rates near historical highs.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
ANTD.VN - Interest rates on corporate bond issuances in general have approached the peak levels of the 2022-2023 period, with the banking sector surpassing this peak.
According to S&I Ratings' observations, corporate bond issuance activity slowed down in Q3 2026 with only 153 successful issuances, totaling VND 179.4 trillion, a sharp decrease of 26% compared to Q2. However, compared to the same period last year, the issuance value increased slightly by 7.8% in Q3 and by 6.7% in the first nine months of the year.
Despite the overall market slowdown, the public offering channel recorded impressive results with 16 successful issuances in the past quarter, equivalent to a total value of VND 31.6 trillion, a 55% increase compared to the same period last year and the highest level ever recorded. Commercial banks remain the dominant issuers and account for the largest share in this form, with 8 out of 16 issuances, mainly valued at VND 1-3 billion, with Agribank alone successfully issuing VND 15,000 billion.
In the first nine months of the year, a cumulative total of 464.1 trillion VND of corporate bonds were issued. Meanwhile, the value of maturing and early repurchased bonds was 132.8 trillion VND (+5.7%) and 228.6 trillion VND (-4.5%), respectively, resulting in a net bond issuance value of 102.6 trillion VND.
Thus, the total value of outstanding bonds increased only slightly by 7.1% compared to the end of 2025, reaching 1.54 trillion VND.
Compared to a GDP growth rate of 9% in the first nine months of 2026 and credit growth of 11.59%, the corporate bond market is expected to grow relatively slowly in 2026.
According to S&I Ratings, high credit demand has driven interest rates up sharply, significantly impacting the cost of capital for businesses. In addition, businesses need to prepare for stricter compliance requirements after Decree 200/2026/ND-CP is issued and takes effect on June 5, 2026.
Bank bond sales slow down, interest rates reach record highs.
In the third quarter, the Real Estate sector failed to maintain the high issuance rate of the second quarter, with the number of successful issuances decreasing from 43 to 21, and the issuance value falling by 55%. Despite this, the issuance volume of this sector in the third quarter still increased by 27% year-on-year, and the cumulative increase for the first nine months of the year was 121% year-on-year.

According to S&I Ratings, on the one hand, the challenging real estate market amidst rising interest rates has significantly impacted project implementation timelines and capital costs for businesses. On the other hand, the substantial capital needs for projects will continue to be a key driver for real estate companies to increase bond issuance in the coming period.
Interest rates on this group of bonds have increased sharply to 12.5% - 13% per year, but are still not as high as the previous peak (14%-14.5% per year).
Meanwhile, bank bond issuance in the quarter reached VND 120 trillion, an increase of 11.8% compared to the same period last year and a 7% increase compared to the previous quarter. However, the cumulative issuance volume for the first nine months was still 20% lower than the same period last year.
According to S&I Ratings, the new LDR calculation method under Circular 50 (which only allows bonds meeting Tier 2 capital requirements to be included in the LDR denominator) has somewhat reduced the incentive for commercial banks to issue bonds.
In the third quarter, coupon interest rates of the banking group ranged from 8% to 9.7% per year, averaging 8.85% per year, officially surpassing the 2022 peak (average 8.7% per year, highest 9.7% per year).
Notably, some of the highest-paying bond issuances have exceeded 10% per year, such as those of SACOMBANK (fixed interest rate of 10% per year) and PVcomBank (average 12-month personal savings interest rate + 4.6% per year, currently equivalent to approximately 10.4% per year).
Overall, corporate bond coupon rates have increased by an average of 250 basis points; however, the rate of increase slowed significantly in the third quarter as interest rates approached their peak levels for the 2022-2023 period.
Pressure to meet maturity continues to mount.
Entering the fourth quarter of 2026, pressure from corporate bond maturing will increase significantly as the total value of bonds due for payment is estimated at approximately 93 trillion VND, the highest level of the year. Of this, the real estate sector continues to face the greatest pressure, with maturing bonds valued at around 46.9 trillion VND, equivalent to nearly half of the total maturing value of the entire market.
The pressure from maturing bonds is expected to continue increasing in 2027, not just in 2026. According to estimates by S&I Ratings, the total value of corporate bonds maturing in 2027 could reach approximately VND 276 trillion, a 22% increase compared to 2026. Of this, the real estate sector alone accounts for VND 156 trillion, equivalent to 57% of the total market value maturing.

Therefore, future new issuances will not only aim to meet the capital raising needs for new projects but also play a crucial role in restructuring existing debts.
Besides the pressure of maturity, the economy 's demand for medium and long-term capital is entering a strong growth cycle to serve a series of large-scale real estate, urban development, transportation infrastructure, energy, and industrial projects. In this context, corporate bonds are expected to continue to be an important capital mobilization channel to supplement medium and long-term resources for the economy.
However, the market's capacity to absorb capital may be affected by the context of persistently high global and domestic interest rates. The lingering risks to inflation expectations, coupled with the trend of high international government bond yields, could keep interest rates high for at least the first half of 2027.

articles.summary: Vietnam moves to standardise digital economy measurement  Vietnam+ (VietnamPlus)
articles.full_text:
Hanoi (VNA) – Deputy Prime Minister Ho Quoc Dung chaired a meeting with the Ministry of Science and Technology (MOST) and the Ministry of Finance (MOF) on October 21 to agree on an indicator and methodology for measuring the digital economy’s contribution to GDP. 
The digital economy is a strategic priority for Vietnam, which aims to raise its share of GDP to at least 30% by 2030, in line with the Politburo’s Resolution No. 57-NQ/TW on breakthroughs in science and technology, innovation and national digital transformation, according to the MOST. Accurately assessing progress towards this target requires unified indicators, measurement methods and official data sources to objectively reflect the digital economy’s contribution to economic growth. 
At the meeting, participants discussed the implementation of digital economy indicators under Party and Government resolutions, focusing on definitions, calculation methods and the responsibilities of relevant agencies. They also considered indicators for assessing progress in 2027 and setting a course towards the 2030 target. 
After hearing reports from ministries and agencies, Deputy PM Dung assigned the MOST to coordinate with the MOF to agree on the indicator’s name for measuring, monitoring and assessing the digital economy’s contribution to GDP. 
The two ministries were also tasked with clarifying the indicator’s definition, scope and measurement approach, and establishing a consistent methodology for identifying and measuring the digital economy before reporting to the Prime Minister. 
Dung stressed the need to standardise terminology, methodologies and statistical indicators to provide a sound basis for monitoring and evaluating progress towards national digital economy development targets. 
According to the National Statistics Office under the MOF, the digital economy’s share of GDP, measured by value added, increased from 12.87% in 2021 to 14.02% in 2025. Vietnam aims to raise the figure to 14.5% in 2026 under the Government’s annual work plan on science and technology, innovation, digital transformation and Project 06./.

articles.title: Vietnam corporate bond market slows as interest rates rise - Theinvestor
articles.summary: Vietnam corporate bond market slows as interest rates rise  Theinvestor
articles.full_text:
Vietnam’s corporate bond market slowed in the third quarter of 2026, with issuance value falling 26% from the previous quarter, while issuance yields continued to rise across all sectors.
Bond issuance slows
According to a recent report by S&I Ratings, Vietnam’s corporate bond market recorded 153 successful issuances in the third quarter, with a total value of VND179.4 trillion ($6.93 billion), down 26% from the second quarter.
The trend mirrored 2025, when issuance surged in Q2 following a sluggish start to the year before correcting in Q3.
Year-on-year, issuance value in Q3 rose 7.8%, while the cumulative increase for the first nine months reached 6.7%.
Notably, public bond offerings performed strongly, with 16 successful issuances in Q3 worth a combined VND31.6 trillion ($1.22 billion), up 55% year-on-year and the highest level on record.
Commercial banks continued to dominate this channel, accounting for eight of the 16 offerings. Individual issuances were mostly valued at VND1 trillion to VND3 trillion ($115.93 million), while Agribank alone successfully issued VND15 trillion.
In the first nine months, total corporate bond issuance reached VND464.1 trillion ($17.93 billion). During the same period, bonds worth VND132.8 trillion ($5.13 billion) matured, up 5.7%, while early bond buybacks totalled VND228.6 trillion, down 4.5%. Net issuance value was reported at VND102.6 trillion ($8.83 billion).
As of the end of September 2026, outstanding corporate bonds totalled approximately VND1,540 trillion ($59.51 billion), up 7.1% from the end of 2025.
According to S&I Ratings, real estate bond issuance corrected in Q3 after surging in Q2. The number of successful issuances fell from 43 to 21, while total issuance value dropped 55% quarter-on-quarter.
The decline was mainly driven by changes in fundraising activity among major corporate groups. Issuance by the Vingroup group fell to VND16 trillion ($618.3 million) in Q3 from VND61 trillion in the previous quarter. Meanwhile, the Masterise group maintained issuance at VND23.5 trillion ($908.14 million) in Q3.
The ratings agency said the two corporations typically account for as much as 80% of total issuance by the real estate sector, giving their fundraising activity a significant influence on the industry's overall performance.
Despite the sharp quarterly decline, real estate bond issuance in Q3 was still up 27% from a year earlier. For the first nine months as a whole, issuance increased 121% year-on-year.
S&I Ratings noted the real estate market was facing difficulties amid rising interest rates, which were affecting project implementation schedules and companies' financing costs. However, substantial funding requirements for project development would remain a key driver of real estate firms' bond fundraising in the coming period.
In the banking sector, total bond issuance reached VND120 trillion ($4.64 million) in Q3, up 11.8% year-on-year and 7% from Q2. However, cumulative issuance in the first nine months remained 20% below the same period in 2025.
With banks accounting for around two-thirds of total corporate bond issuance, the sector's decline was also a key factor behind the market's slower growth.
Issuance rates approach 2022-2023 peaks
Corporate bond issuance rates continued to rise across all sectors in Q3/2026. Coupon rates had increased by an average of around 250 basis points from their 2025 lows. However, the pace of increase slowed considerably in Q3 as rates approached the peaks recorded in 2022-2023.
For banks, the average issuance rate reached 8.85% per year in Q3, exceeding the 2022 average of 8.7%. However, it remained below the previous peak of 9.7%.
Bank bond coupon rates in Q3 generally ranged from 8% to 9.7% per year. Some issuances carried rates of 10% or higher, including Sacombank bonds with a fixed coupon of 10% and PVcomBank bonds paying a rate linked to the average 12-month savings deposit rate for individual customers plus a margin of 4.6 percentage points, equivalent to around 10.4% at the time of the report.
Meanwhile, issuance rates for real estate companies and firms in other sectors also rose sharply, reaching around 12.5-13% per year. Even so, these rates remained below the peak range of 14-14.5% recorded in 2022-2023.
The trend highlights continued increases in bond fundraising costs as interest rates approach levels last seen during the previous high-rate period.
Maturity pressures to rise in late 2026 and 2027
Maturity pressures in Vietnam's corporate bond market are expected to increase significantly in Q4/2026. S&I Ratings estimates that bonds worth around VND93 trillion ($3.59 billion) will fall due for repayment during the quarter, the highest amount for any quarter this year. Real estate companies account for approximately VND46.9 trillion ($1.81 billion), or nearly half of the market's total maturities.
The pressure is expected to intensify further in 2027. Total corporate bonds maturing next year could reach around VND276 trillion ($10.67 billion), up 22% from 2026. Real estate companies alone are expected to face approximately VND156 trillion ($6.03 billion) in maturities, accounting for 57% of the market total.
Against this backdrop, new bond issuance will serve not only to finance projects but also to play an important role in restructuring existing debt.
Beyond refinancing pressures, the economy's medium- and long-term funding needs are entering a period of strong growth to support real estate developments, urban areas, transport infrastructure, energy and industrial projects. Corporate bonds are therefore expected to remain an important funding channel, providing additional medium- and long-term capital to the economy.
However, the market's ability to absorb new issuance could be affected by domestic and international interest rate movements. Persistent inflation risks, coupled with international government bond yields remaining elevated, could keep interest rates high at least through the first half of 2027.
For bond issuers, this would mean higher financing costs, particularly for companies with high leverage or substantial funding needs.
S&I Ratings said the medium-term outlook for Vietnam's corporate bond market remained positive, supported by strong corporate funding demand and mounting refinancing pressures.
Nevertheless, with interest rates still high, the market would need more time to continue restructuring on a sustainable basis, attract a broader range of investors, and strengthen its role as a key source of medium- and long-term financing for the economy.

articles.title: MetaComp wins Singapore Financial Innovation of the Year - Financial Technology at the Asian Innovation Excellence Awards 2026 - Asian Business Review
articles.summary: MetaComp wins Singapore Financial Innovation of the Year - Financial Technology at the Asian Innovation Excellence Awards 2026  Asian Business Review
articles.full_text:
The StableX Agentic Network brings fiat and stablecoin rails into one hybrid network and sets out how AI agents can make payments with clear accountability.
MetaComp Pte. Ltd. (MetaComp) has won Singapore Financial Innovation of the Year – Financial Technology at the Asian Innovation Excellence Awards 2026 for the StableX Agentic Network.
Slow corridors
Cross-border payments are still slow for businesses. MetaComp’s 2025 research on ASEAN SMEs, found that international wire transfers can take two to seven days, and that these delays can cost businesses more than the fees themselves.
The StableX Agentic Network
MetaComp’s answer is hybrid payments. Headquartered in Singapore and licensed by the Monetary Authority of Singapore as a Major Payment Institution, MetaComp built the StableX Agentic Network to connect fiat and stablecoin rails through a compliant Web2.5 architecture. The network brings five capabilities together:
Payments
The network connects fiat and stablecoin rails, giving businesses more than one way to move money across borders, so a slow or unavailable corridor need not hold up a transaction.
FX routing
For each transaction, the routing engine evaluates fiat and stablecoin pathways and selects a route based on applicable routing parameters, including rate.
Compliance intelligence
The VisionX Engine brings fiat and on-chain intelligence together. It draws on multiple independent blockchain analytics providers and reconciles their outputs through a proprietary methodology. Compliance teams get one consistent view of risk across both environments, in support of anti-money laundering and counter-financing of terrorism (AML/CFT) requirements.
Agent governance
The StableX Know Your Agent (KYA) Framework sets out how AI agents are identified, what they are permitted to do, how their behaviour is monitored, and who is accountable for them.
Wealth and treasury
Eligible clients can access wealth and treasury solutions, including Alpha Ladder WealthX, offered separately by Alpha Ladder Finance Pte. Ltd., MetaComp’s affiliate, which holds a Capital Markets Services licence.
The network now counts more than 1,000 members and more than 100,000 users.
Agentic Finance
In 2026, MetaComp began extending the network into agentic finance, where AI agents carry out financial tasks on behalf of people and businesses.
AgentX, introduced in March, lets AI agents on compatible platforms access MetaComp’s compliance intelligence and payment capabilities through downloadable skills. The first skill screens wallet addresses across multiple know-your-transaction (KYT) databases.
In April, at Money20/20 Asia in Bangkok, MetaComp launched the StableX Know Your Agent (KYA) Framework for Agentic Finance. KYA was designed in alignment with IMDA’s Model AI Governance Framework for Agentic AI. It has since been productised and updated with reference to MAS’s Safeguards for Agentic Finance at Runtime (SAFR) white paper, setting out how agents are identified, what they are permitted to do, how their behaviour is monitored, and who is accountable for them.
“This recognition belongs to everyone building the StableX Agentic Network with us,” said Tin Pei Ling, Co-President, MetaComp. “Payments innovation is measured by trust as much as speed, and that test gets harder as AI agents start paying on our behalf. Just as each of us carries a passport, an agent paying for someone should carry an identity that can be verified, with a human accountable behind it. If you can risk-rate a human, you can risk-rate an agent. That is what the StableX Know Your Agent Framework is designed to do. Standards cannot sit behind walled gardens. We invite payment service providers and financial institutions to build this network with us, and we look forward to sharing what comes next.”
MetaComp plans to grow the network’s membership and deepen its agentic capabilities as more platforms support agent-callable financial services, and welcomes payment service providers, financial institutions and businesses to join.
