articles.title: A number of banks have reduced lending rates. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: A number of banks have reduced lending rates.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
Commercial banks are implementing interest rate reductions on loans as requested by the State Bank of Vietnam, but more coordinated solutions are needed to ensure this policy is more widespread across the market.
Following directives from the Government and the State Bank of Vietnam (SBV) on stabilizing and reducing lending interest rates, a number of banks have announced interest rate reductions. Specifically, Agribank reduced lending interest rates by 2% per year compared to normal rates, focusing on priority sectors and production and business customers, contributing to reducing capital cost pressure and creating conditions for businesses and individuals to maintain and expand operations and develop the economy according to the set targets. Simultaneously, Agribank continues to implement a 70,000 billion VND credit program for small and medium-sized enterprises, priority sectors, and new growth drivers with lending interest rates 1-2% lower per year than the average lending interest rate for the same term. Meanwhile, BIDV announced the implementation of a credit package of approximately 100,000 billion VND, with loan terms up to 6 months and interest rate reductions of 1.5-2%, bringing lending interest rates down to 6-7% depending on the term. Simultaneously, Vietcombank announced a reduction in lending interest rates of 1.5 - 2% per year, with short-term lending rates reduced by up to 3% per year for certain sectors compared to the usual rate. In parallel, the bank also reduced savings interest rates by 0.5% per year.
Similarly, VietinBank implemented a reduction in lending interest rates of up to 2% per year, prioritizing resources for key sectors and growth drivers in the last months of 2026; MB reduced interest rates by 1.5% per year for 5 priority sectors, with lending rates starting from 7.9% per year. In particular, for some priority cases, MB considered applying a reduction of up to 2% per year, creating more favorable conditions for businesses and individuals to access credit at reasonable costs.
Many other commercial banks also participated in this interest rate reduction, such as Vietbank, which allocated 3,000 billion VND for loans with interest rates 1.5% lower per year than usual; Sacombank implemented a 40,000 billion VND credit package, reducing lending interest rates by 2% per year, with preferential rates starting from 8.5% per year for domestic businesses operating in key sectors that need additional capital for production and business; import-export businesses and foreign-invested enterprises (FDI). LPBank also announced a 1.6-2% per year reduction in lending interest rates for new disbursements serving short-term production and business for individuals, household businesses, and micro-enterprises from now until the end of the year. In addition to lending interest rates, some banks such as Vietbank and BVBank also reduced deposit interest rates by 0.5-0.6% per year for terms of 6 months or more.
Only when inflation is controlled within the target can monetary policy be applied flexibly, finding a balance between supporting growth and maintaining macroeconomic stability. At that point, the State Bank of Vietnam will also have room to apply various tools to support liquidity for banks, inject capital into the economy, and contribute to reducing lending interest rates.
Economist, Member of Parliament , Associate Professor, Dr. Tran Hoang Ngan
At a meeting with leaders of commercial banks yesterday morning, October 20th, Governor of the State Bank of Vietnam, Pham Duc An, stated that to genuinely reduce lending interest rates, banks must simultaneously cut operating costs, share profits, and reduce the cost of capital mobilization. Continuing to push deposit interest rates higher will make it difficult to justify reducing lending interest rates. Banks also need to note that interest rate reductions should not be indiscriminate but should be selective, balanced with the financial capacity of each bank, and should consider both existing and new loans. The State Bank of Vietnam will continue to support banks in implementing these measures, but without compromising the safety of the system.
More policies are needed to reduce interest rates.
You may also like
Economist, National Assembly representative, Associate Professor Dr. Tran Hoang Ngan believes that the State Bank of Vietnam's (SBV) implementation of specific solutions and requirements for credit institutions at this time is extremely urgent, aiming to help businesses reduce capital costs. To achieve this goal, the SBV first needs to strengthen supervision to ensure commercial banks strictly comply with regulations. Simultaneously, if permitted, the SBV should increase liquidity and provide capital to banks through the interbank market, and be ready to refinance key and large-scale projects. At the same time, the regulatory body could also signal its willingness to increase lending capacity for institutions that comply well with regulations, especially by reducing lending interest rates. This would also give banks more room to lend towards the end of the year.
However, while monetary policy plays a crucial role in capital supply and macroeconomic stability, it cannot single-handedly address all of the economy's capital needs. Therefore, it needs to be combined with fiscal policy to truly achieve effective interest rate reduction. Specifically, Mr. Tran Hoang Ngan analyzed: The government still has room to implement expansionary fiscal policy as public debt is only at around 33% of GDP. It is necessary to continue reducing taxes and fees on state-managed goods such as gasoline, healthcare, and education to curb inflation. Based on this, the State Bank of Vietnam will have the confidence and room to implement flexible monetary policy, simultaneously supporting economic growth, controlling inflation, and ensuring the safety of the banking system. "Only when inflation is controlled within the target can monetary policy be applied flexibly, finding a balance between supporting growth and maintaining macroeconomic stability. At that point, the State Bank of Vietnam will also have room to apply more tools to support liquidity for banks, inject capital into the economy, and contribute to reducing lending interest rates," Associate Professor Tran Hoang Ngan shared.
According to the Governor of the State Bank of Vietnam, Pham Duc An, as of the end of last week, capital mobilization increased by 11.22% and credit increased by 11.44%; the difference between outstanding loans and capital mobilization in VND, which was previously nearly 2 trillion VND, has now decreased to below 1.5 trillion VND. As of October 14th, outstanding credit to the economy reached 20,721 trillion VND, an increase of 11.44% compared to the end of the previous year and an increase of 16.73% compared to the same period last year.
Meanwhile, Associate Professor Pham The Anh, Head of the Economics Department at the National Economics University, analyzed: to reduce lending interest rates, it is necessary to look at the issue of capital allocation in the economy. Capital is limited, so when capital is concentrated in a group of projects or businesses, the amount of capital available for other entities will decrease. For example, if a lot of capital is concentrated in large public investment projects or projects of large corporations, the remaining capital available for small and medium-sized enterprises, especially manufacturing businesses, will be less. The policy of reducing lending interest rates for priority sectors is a good direction, but its implementation in practice still faces challenges due to the profit motives of banks and the market-based capital allocation mechanism.
From there, Mr. Pham The Anh noted a crucial issue currently: the accumulation of unsold real estate and bad debts arising from the real estate market. For many years, the relatively easy expansion of credit has contributed to the promotion of real estate speculation. As a result, a large amount of capital is tied up in high-value but illiquid real estate assets, including assets owned by project developers and assets held by speculators. When real estate is difficult to sell, cash flow stagnates. To unblock capital flow, it is necessary to address the accumulated assets and related bad debts. For assets secured by bad debts, liquidation or foreclosure may be one of the necessary measures. For developers with large inventories, they need to consider adjusting selling prices to a market-acceptable level to sell their products, recover funds, and regenerate capital. However, reducing lending interest rates depends not only on handling bad debts but also on the scale of capital, credit growth rate, capital needs of large projects, and the capital allocation mechanisms of banks.
Capital market development
Financial expert Nguyen Tri Hieu analyzed Vietnam's credit-to-GDP ratio at approximately 150%, indicating a high level of dependence of businesses on bank credit, as the capital market is not yet deep enough to provide alternative financing sources. When banks are the primary source of capital, changes in banking practices, such as interest rates, can directly impact businesses' access to capital, investment progress, and economic growth. Expanding credit availability could provide additional impetus for short-term economic growth, but it also necessitates ensuring the safety of the banking system and diversifying capital supply channels. While the capital market is not yet strong enough to share the burden of financing for the economy, banks still have to meet the majority of businesses' capital needs, including medium- and long-term investments.

The Hanoi Department of Industry and Trade, in coordination with the Vietnam Trade Office in Hong Kong and relevant agencies, has set up a Vietnamese pavilion with 20 booths of 20 enterprises. Exhibits include lacquerware, rattan and bamboo crafts, ceramics, horn handicrafts and premium gifts, all among Vietnam’s key export products.
Hoang Minh Lam, Director of the department’s Industry and Trade Promotion Centre, said MEGA SHOW is one of the major specialised trade fairs that attracts international importers and buyers, and serves as a key sourcing hub in the Asia-Pacific region.
The expo gives Hanoi-based businesses and rural industrial establishments a chance to promote their brands, showcase their production capacity, connect with foreign partners, expand distribution networks and increase handicraft exports, he said.
Nguyen Ngoc Anh, head of the export–import division from Doan Ket 1 Co., Ltd, said the company’s booth, which entirely showcases handmade handicrafts produced by traditional craft villages in Phu Nghia commune of Hanoi, attracted a large number of international visitors and those seeking business opportunities.

articles.title: Two years into presidency, Indonesia’s Prabowo faces tough balancing act between ambitious promises and fiscal discipline - CNA
articles.summary: Two years into presidency, Indonesia’s Prabowo faces tough balancing act between ambitious promises and fiscal discipline  CNAIn charts: Indonesia’s Prabowo Subianto misses beat on economy  Financial TimesIndonesia economy strong on paper, but people struggling  Asia News NetworkPrabowo Government Gets Poor Ratings from 66% of Surveyed Professionals  Jakarta GlobeTwo Years into the Prabowo-Gibran Presidency, IESR Urges Improvements in Fuel Supply and Elect...
articles.full_text:
As Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto enters his third year in office, observers say the challenge will be to translate his ambitious promises into tangible results while balancing public expectations with economic and political stability.
DEPOK, Indonesia: Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto marked two years in office on Tuesday (Oct 20), with his administration touting progress on food security and energy independence, even as questions mount over the sustainability of his ambitious social welfare programmes.
Since taking office in October 2024, Mr Prabowo has made sweeping promises to improve the lives of ordinary Indonesians, with his administration highlighting rice self-sufficiency, progress towards greater energy independence and stronger-than-expected economic growth as key achievements.
But as he enters his third year in office, the former military general faces a challenge to deliver lasting benefits without undermining Indonesia's fiscal stability.
Political manoeuvring is also expected to intensify ahead of the 2029 general election, potentially testing the durability of his broad ruling coalition.
AMBITIOUS WELFARE PLANS COME AT A COST
Among the latest proposals being considered by the government is the abolition of tuition fees at state universities nationwide.
Last month, Mr Prabowo instructed the Ministry of Higher Education, Science and Technology to develop a framework for providing free education at public universities.
Some students believe greater access to higher education deserves greater priority in the national budget.
“Spending on other programmes … such as the president’s flagship free meals programme … is much higher. I believe education should also be a priority when it comes to how our government spends its revenue,” said Isyana Balqis, an undergraduate at the University of Indonesia.
Her fellow schoolmate Amanda Putri Dimas said: “I have to work while studying to cover my tuition and other expenses. If Indonesia truly wants to achieve its Golden Indonesia vision, this should have been planned from the very beginning. I hope this plan will actually become a reality.”
The Golden Indonesia 2045 vision aims to transform the country into an advanced economy by the centenary of its independence, with education seen as key to developing a more skilled workforce.
However, the proposal comes with a substantial price tag.
The government estimates that eliminating tuition fees for nearly 3 million undergraduate and diploma students at state universities would require an additional 93 trillion rupiah (US$5 billion) annually, roughly US$1,850 per student.
While the plan has generated optimism, it has also prompted questions about how the government intends to finance another major spending commitment.
FREE MEALS PROGRAMME UNDER SCRUTINY
At the centre of Mr Prabowo's welfare agenda is his flagship free nutritious meals programme, aimed at combating stunting and malnutrition among children.
Despite food poisoning incidents that have raised concerns over food safety and oversight, the initiative has expanded rapidly to reach more than 57 million beneficiaries nationwide, including schoolchildren, toddlers, breastfeeding mothers and pregnant women.
At least US$15 billion has been earmarked for the initiative in next year's state budget, underscoring the significant financial resources required to sustain it and intensifying scrutiny of the government's spending priorities as it simultaneously pursues other costly programmes.
Indonesia’s parliament in September approved Mr Prabowo’s 2027 budget, with spending projected at over US$228 billion.
The growing expenditure has also revived debate over Indonesia's long-standing fiscal rules.
The country's annual budget deficit is capped at 3 per cent of gross domestic product, a restriction intended to maintain fiscal discipline and reassure investors.
Some lawmakers have called for a review of that ceiling to give the government greater flexibility to spend.
However, critics warn that relaxing the limit could weaken confidence in Indonesia's fiscal management.
“That's very risky because it implies that the government will do anything to raise funds for these priority programmes or projects,” said Bhima Yudhistira Adhinegara, executive director of the Centre of Economic and Law Studies (CELIOS), a Jakarta-based public policy institution.
“The consequence is that investors and creditors may start to view Indonesia as being a little reckless.”
Last Friday (16 Oct), Indonesian stocks suffered their steepest one-day fall in nearly three decades, after index provider MSCI raised the prospect of stripping the country of its “emerging market” status.
ECONOMIC GROWTH OFFERS BRIGHT SPOT
Despite concerns over government spending, Indonesia's economy has shown resilience.
The economy expanded by 5.45 per cent in the first half of 2026, exceeding economists' expectations and prompting the International Monetary Fund (IMF) to raise its full-year growth forecast.
However, a significant portion of that expansion has been driven by public expenditure, raising questions about whether the momentum can be sustained.
Government spending rose 15.97 per cent in the second quarter, following an even sharper increase of 21.81 per cent in Q1.
Analysts say that while higher public spending can stimulate economic activity in the short term, sustained growth will also require stronger private investment, job creation and productivity gains.
That is particularly important for Mr Prabowo, who has set an ambitious target of accelerating Indonesia's economic growth to 8 per cent annually.
Last month, Mr Prabowo appointed Mr Suahasil Nazara as finance minister, placing him at the centre of efforts to balance the administration's spending ambitions with fiscal discipline.
Mr Suahasil has pledged to maintain the budget deficit below the statutory ceiling of 3 per cent of GDP, signalling continuity in the government's commitment to fiscal prudence.
However, the pressure to finance expensive welfare initiatives, infrastructure development and other national priorities could test that commitment in the years ahead.
CABINET SHAKE-UPS RAISE POLITICAL QUESTIONS
Economic challenges are not the only pressures confronting Mr Prabowo as he begins the second half of his five-year presidential term.
This month, he carried out his seventh and largest cabinet reshuffle, replacing several high-profile figures overseeing key economic, diplomatic and security portfolios.
Political observers say the shake-ups could be aimed at tightening his grip on the ruling coalition and ensuring that ministers remain aligned with his priorities, amid signs of declining public approval.
They caution that the coalition's cohesion could face growing challenges as political parties begin positioning themselves for the 2029 general election, especially if public dissatisfaction with the administration grows.
“Part of the reason why the coalition is so intact now is because everybody is compliant with Mr Prabowo … because they expect political incentives,” said Mr Djayadi Hanan, head of the political science programme at Indonesian International Islamic University.
“With the fact that the public is having more and more gap with the president, indicated at least by the very low approval rating, the political parties (looking ahead at) the next election will think (if) it’s worth it being on the side of the president.”
Further complications could emerge from efforts by some political parties to impeach Vice President Gibran Rakabuming Raka. Mr Gibran, the eldest son of former president Joko Widodo, has faced growing scrutiny over his educational credentials.
The Constitutional Court has dismissed a legal challenge seeking his disqualification on procedural grounds, but continued questions surrounding his vice presidency could become another source of political tension.
The issue is particularly sensitive given Mr Gibran's ties to his father, whose support played a significant role in the political alliance that brought Mr Prabowo to power in 2024.
HAZE CLOUDING FOREIGN RELATIONS
Beyond economic and political pressures, the administration is also grappling with a major environmental crisis.
Forest and land fires have been raging across parts of Indonesia for more than two months, triggering transboundary haze and raising concerns about air quality across the region.
More than 60,000 firefighters have been deployed to contain the blazes.
Indonesia has long struggled with recurring forest and peatland fires, particularly during prolonged dry periods. The resulting haze poses public health risks, disrupts economic activity and can strain diplomatic relations with neighbouring countries.
During a hybrid limited cabinet meeting last week, Mr Prabowo described the crisis as one of his administration's highest priorities and pledged to strengthen preventive measures.
“If there are any needs or requirements, tell us what you need. This is one of our highest priorities. We must address this immediately, and we must prevent it from happening again. Going forward, our campaign and strategy must be extensive, comprehensive and far-reaching, with a strong focus on prevention,” he said.
He has replaced the head of the agency responsible for firefighting and disaster relief, put in place directives against slash-and-burn practices on peatland, and prioritised fire prevention as a long-term solution.
As Mr Prabowo enters his third year in office, the challenge will be to translate his ambitious promises into tangible results while balancing public expectations with economic and political stability.
And with the 2029 election approaching, his ability to deliver could prove crucial to maintaining public confidence and the support of his political allies.

articles.title: With low liquidity, real estate transactions are predicted to pick up again in the fourth quarter. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: With low liquidity, real estate transactions are predicted to pick up again in the fourth quarter.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
The real estate market is projected to see a doubling of housing transactions in the fourth quarter of 2026 compared to the previous quarter, although liquidity remains low. However, high borrowing interest rates, unaffordable home prices, and cautious buyer sentiment make the prospect of recovery challenging.
Expectations for a sharp increase in trading volume, but liquidity remains uneven.
According to forecasts by the Vietnam Association of Real Estate Brokers (VARS), the volume of housing transactions in the fourth quarter of 2026 could double compared to the third quarter. The prospect of economic growth, public investment disbursement, foreign direct investment (FDI) inflows, and remittances at the end of the year are expected to provide further impetus to the market.
Besides seasonal factors, the need for stable housing for families and improvements in the supply of social housing could also support liquidity. In the secondary market, transactions are expected to increase as the demand for relocation in major cities continues to exist.
However, the positive outlook for the final quarter of the year does not necessarily mean the market has recovered uniformly. Developments in Hanoi during the third quarter show that purchasing power remains under considerable pressure.
According to CBRE's market report, Hanoi recorded over 3,900 apartments sold in Q3 2026, a 33% decrease compared to the previous quarter and a 66% decrease compared to the same period in 2025. This is the lowest level since Q1 2024.
The average asking price for secondary apartments in Hanoi has also fallen to around 60 million VND/m², down 5% quarter-on-quarter and 8% year-on-year. Meanwhile, floating interest rates at some commercial banks, at 13-15% per year, continue to put pressure on homebuyers using borrowed capital.
This reality shows that demand hasn't completely disappeared, but the gap between the need to find housing and the ability to convert it into a transaction remains significant. Buyers tend to consider more carefully the selling price, project legal aspects, handover schedule, and repayment capacity before deciding to make a purchase.
On the supply side, VARS forecasts that the volume of new commercial housing launched in the fourth quarter may be equivalent to the third quarter. Businesses still face pressure from capital, interest costs, and cautious customer sentiment.
You may also like
The supply in the suburbs of Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City continues to be concentrated in large-scale urban areas with integrated infrastructure, primarily consisting of apartments and townhouses. Several other localities such as Da Nang, Bac Ninh , Quang Ninh, and Hai Phong are expected to see the addition of new properties.
For social housing, increasing supply can provide further impetus to the market, especially for those with genuine housing needs. However, the number of projects being implemented does not mean that all units are ready for sale or have reached buyers. The actual effectiveness depends on the completion progress, pricing, and accessibility for the right target beneficiaries.
Housing prices and affordability determine market resilience.
According to experts, one of the biggest challenges facing the market today is the gap between property prices and buyers' financial capacity. Even if transactions increase towards the end of the year, the market will struggle to achieve a sustainable recovery if house prices remain high while borrowing costs continue to burden households.
Associate Professor Ngo Tri Long, an economic expert from the Vietnam Financial Consulting Association, noted that high interest rates are putting pressure on purchasing power and liquidity. Meanwhile, asking prices are not easily adjusted quickly due to land costs, construction costs, financing costs, and seller expectations.
This has resulted in uneven price adjustments. In some areas, sellers may have to lower their expectations to find buyers, while new projects maintain high prices. Therefore, the increase in the number of transactions is not enough to confirm that the entire market has entered a new recovery cycle.
To improve liquidity, developers can continue to apply discount policies, interest rate subsidies, or payment schedule extensions. However, the effectiveness of these policies needs to be evaluated based on their ability to reduce actual costs for customers, rather than just creating initial appeal during the sales period.
You may also like
For homebuyers, the financial equation isn't just about the price of the apartment. Monthly loan payments, interest rates after the preferential period, living expenses, and income stability all directly impact the decision to buy a home. In the context of high interest rates, taking out excessively large loans can cause many families to continue delaying transactions, even though the need for housing remains.
From a business perspective, projects with transparent legal frameworks, guaranteed progress, convenient infrastructure connections, and prices suitable for their target customer group will have an advantage. The market also needs more products that meet real housing needs, rather than relying too heavily on expectations of future price increases.
Another important indicator is price and transaction activity in the secondary market. The asking price may not fully reflect the price that buyers are actually willing to pay. Therefore, it is necessary to simultaneously monitor the volume of successful transactions, the absorption rate, and the gap between the asking price and the actual transaction price to more accurately assess the health of the market.
VARS' forecast that housing transactions in the fourth quarter will double compared to the third quarter is a noteworthy signal, but it still needs to be verified by actual results. In the long term, sustainable recovery depends not only on the number of products brought to the market, but also on the ability to meet real housing needs, reasonable prices, and people's access to housing.

Accordingly, the Ho Chi Minh City Real Estate Association (HoREA) highly welcomes Circular No. 50/2026 of the State Bank of Vietnam, which allows credit institutions to use up to 95% of their mobilized capital for lending.
Recently, Governor of the State Bank of Vietnam, Pham Duc An, chaired a meeting with credit institutions and issued decisive directives to reduce interest rates to support businesses and the economy . Commercial banks must reduce listed savings deposit interest rates by at least 0.5% per year for terms of 6 months or more, absolutely avoiding a race to increase deposit interest rates, and must reduce lending interest rates by 1.5% to 2% per year to focus on supporting production, business, and priority sectors.
This applies to both new loans and existing outstanding loans (old loans) and is implemented on the basis that credit institutions must reduce operating costs and share bank profits, but absolutely must not lower credit standards or compromise asset quality to increase lending scale.

According to Mr. Le Hoang Chau, Chairman of HoREA, this is the first time the Governor of the State Bank of Vietnam has requested credit institutions to share the bank's profits, rather than just making a general call for reducing bank operating costs to lower lending interest rates.
Because banks are very concerned about reducing operating costs, and the directive from the Governor of the State Bank of Vietnam has been agreed upon by the leaders of all banks, the four largest commercial banks (Big 4) and many other credit institutions have responded and immediately implemented interest rate reductions to "share the burden" with borrowers.
Mr. Le Hoang Chau argued that, both logically and morally, it is unacceptable for most of the 27 commercial banks to consistently achieve relatively high and stable annual profits, usually around 7-10 billion USD/year.
Compared to the total charter capital of these 27 banks, which is known to be around 922,000 billion VND, the average profit achieved is approximately 19.7% to 28.2% per year, while businesses still have to borrow at high interest rates, even reaching 18-19% per year in some cases, as reflected in the recent meeting of the Central Steering Committee on Housing Policy and Real Estate Market.
In addition, some credit institutions undervalue collateral for loans, often only about 70% of its actual value, and in some cases, the value of this collateral may be even lower. Credit institutions also have the right to seize collateral for bad debts, so borrowers often suffer losses.

"We highly appreciate the State Bank and the Government's decision to exclude outstanding loans for social housing projects and national key projects (including tourism and resort projects) from the credit growth targets of those banks due to their low risk level. However, we propose that the State Bank and the Government consider applying this mechanism to rental housing projects, affordable commercial housing projects, and some key industrial park projects as proposed by each locality, based on risk classification for each type of real estate project, rather than assuming the entire real estate sector is inherently risky, in order to achieve double-digit GDP growth and tightly control risky sectors," Mr. Le Hoang Chau suggested.

articles.title: Innovation: Choose your job - choose your team - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: Innovation: Choose your job - choose your team  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
In the current innovation landscape, there's a familiar pattern: building numerous centers, signing countless memoranda of understanding, and organizing numerous workshops. The numbers are easy to count, the images are appealing. But after the ribbon-cutting ceremonies, the question of "what products have been created, and how much has it contributed to growth?" often lacks a clear answer.
 Deputy Prime Minister Ho Quoc Dung 's conclusion on the national innovation ecosystem, as stated in Announcement No. 538/TB-VPCP dated October 20, 2026, correctly identifies the root cause of the problem. While the ecosystem has been formed, it has yet to become the primary driver of double-digit growth.
 The bottleneck lies not in a lack of ideas or policies, but in the implementation phase, that is, the transformation of knowledge, technology, finance, and markets into products.
 The "remedy" was also clearly prescribed: developing a network of innovation centers that "doesn't chase quantity," but focuses on efficiency, connectivity, and commercialization.
 Ho Chi Minh City is seeking a solution to this requirement through an approach encapsulated in the phrase "thematic approaches and partnerships." Looking at the models the city is promoting, each center chooses its own "runway."
 The Center of Excellence in Artificial Intelligence (AI COE), launched jointly by SIHUB, the University of Economics Ho Chi Minh City, and Plug and Play, bets on applied AI, using real-world problems from government agencies and businesses as test subjects for startups. Saigon AI Hub, co-founded by VNG and the Vietnam National University Ho Chi Minh City, delves deeper into AI research.
 The 84X program between Block71 and Van Lang University selected only one value chain for the first year: consumption and retail. The High-Tech Park Innovation Center (SHTP-IC) has been restructured, focusing on deep technologies: microchips, robotics, and new materials. SoiHub, a privately invested center, pursues technologies for green growth.
 This role assignment isn't just a technical matter; it can determine whether the centers compete or complement each other. A research group at Saigon AI Hub could become a startup within the AI COE, then introduce their product for controlled testing at SHTP-IC.
 A true network should be like this: each node excels at one task, and the entire network works together to accomplish a larger goal. Without mechanisms for connection and resource sharing, specialization can lead to fragmentation, with each center operating independently, even overlapping and competing for resources.
 The highlight of these models is that international partners are invited to operate them, not just to hold the title. Plug and Play, the world's leading startup accelerator network, provides connections to hundreds of global corporations and investors. Block71, together with the National University of Singapore , contributes expertise in entrepreneurship training and serves as a gateway to Southeast Asia and Japan.
 Notably, the Google AI Futures Fund selected Saigon AI Hub as the first research organization in Vietnam to establish an Applied AI Lab. Here, each center needs a partner with strengths aligned with its specific area of expertise. They possess brand recognition, financial resources, standards, a customer network, and a commitment to achieving results. These are the resources the domestic ecosystem needs to supplement.
 The value of cooperation must be demonstrated by the technology transferred, the commercialized products, and the actual capabilities that Vietnam has accumulated.
 Choosing the right job and the right people isn't enough without internal cohesion. Schools can't just train and "deliver" students to the market; they must shift to collaborative creation.
 Businesses and investment funds should be the ones setting the brief and acting as the initial client. Each commitment needs to be quickly translated into an implementation agreement with a timeline, budget, and targets.
 Evaluation cycles of six months to a year are necessary to ensure results are visible and adjustments can be made promptly. Metrics must be specific: how many projects have been tested, how many application contracts have been signed, how much capital has been raised, and how much personnel have been trained. More importantly, how many products have actually gone into production, are commercially viable, and are creating new value?
 The city also needs a common coordination mechanism so that each center can share problems, experts, investors, and testing space. Then, a startup can simply "enter through one door" and "reach the entire network."
 Effective models should be replicated, while ineffective models must be boldly adjusted, including halting investment if they fail to meet objectives. The results of innovation must be measured by the number of products reaching consumers and the actual value created for the economy .
 Choose fewer tasks, but choose the right ones; choose true companions. The rest is about persevering until the job is done, achieving results, and taking responsibility for those results. Only then can today's specialized centers become a genuine driving force for the city's and the country's double-digit growth targets.
 Choose fewer tasks, but choose the right ones; choose fewer companions, but choose true friends. The rest is about relentlessly seeing things through to the end.
 If successful, these specialized centers will become a real driving force for achieving double-digit growth targets for the city and the country as a whole.

articles.full_text:
Cambodia's Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries (MAFF) is looking into a disaster-related insurance scheme designed for modern agricultural cooperatives.
According to news platform The Khmer Times, MAFF Undersecretary of State and spokesman Khim Finan said that climate change has severely affected Cambodia’s agricultural sector this year, with drought and flooding.
As such, a proposed agricultural insurance mechanism “is intended to help farmers manage losses caused by natural disasters, particularly during the rainy season, when unpredictable weather can threaten crop yields and household incomes”, the article stated.
A preliminary report from the National Committee for Disaster Management that covered July to September showed that drought had destroyed more than 200,000ha of rice crops across 10 provinces. After that, flooding in September impacted about 160,000ha of rice fields across 10 provinces.
Although Cambodia has 40 insurance companies, agricultural insurance remains limited.
